brief: Shoppers are using AI to shortlist, not to decide: 82% of consumers in 17 countries now use it but a third won't let it buy for them, and Havas Market finds a Latin American brand outselling its rival by 25% is mentioned 13 times less by chatbots.

Peak season looks cautious: 59% of US holiday shoppers expect trade-offs and 72% call Black Friday hype, only half of Brazilians plan to buy, and Australian consumer sentiment has hit a four-year low.

In real-world media, WOO warned that OOH bans now spread by precedent, with Hungary clearing Budapest of almost every billboard, while Ocean Outdoor linked Piccadilly Lights with Shibuya's screens in a reciprocal deal with Japan's Hit.

Diary: bids for 12 Delhi Metro stations close on 16 November, oOh!media's scheme returns to court on 18 November, Schiphol's €426m advertising tender closes on 20 November and Northern Railway's Delhi Division advertising e-auction opens on 26 November.

numberOfDay.line: In Latin America, a brand that outsells its rival by 25% is mentioned 13 times less often by AI assistants (Havas Market).

steal.title: Make the host a partner
steal.text: Network X places township billboards at taverns, spaza shops, car washes and clinics, and pays the black-owned businesses that host them a share of ad revenue, plus their electricity and backup power. The idea worth stealing: turn site hosts into stakeholders, so the community looks after and vouches for the media, a model that suits informal retail and neighbourhood networks in any market.

items.headline: Shoppers embrace AI but won't hand it the wallet, VML's 28,000-person Future Shopper study finds
items.dek: Eight in ten consumers across 17 countries now use AI and most check its product picks before buying, yet a third refuse to let it decide, and money worries are sharpening every choice.
items.source: VML, Future Shopper 2026, via HORIZONT

figures.label: Consumers who have used AI (+14 pts in a year)
Check AI product recommendations before buying
Worry commercial interests could bias AI shopping tools
Pay more attention to price than before

keyPoints: 82% of consumers in 17 countries have now used AI, up 14 points in a year, but a third would not let it make a purchase decision on its own.
58% check AI product recommendations before buying, and 53% worry that commercial interests could bias AI shopping tools.
Search is losing goodwill: 44% say search quality has worsened over the past year and 55% say sponsored results make the best products harder to find.
Family remains the strongest purchase influence at 22%, while influencers slipped from 15% to 13%.
Money is tight: 59% are more worried about their finances than ever, 72% watch prices more closely and online's share of spending fell from 53% to 51%.
body: VML's annual Future Shopper study, based on 28,000 consumers in 17 countries plus expert interviews, finds AI firmly embedded in everyday life: 82% have used it, mostly for quick questions and translation. When it comes to shopping, however, consumers treat it as an adviser rather than an agent. 58% verify AI product suggestions before buying, 53% fear commercial interests could steer AI shopping tools and a third would not let AI make purchase decisions unaided.

The study also points to fraying trust in search, with 44% saying results have got worse and 55% saying sponsored listings get in the way. Family members are the most powerful purchase influence (22%), ahead of influencers, whose sway fell to 13%. Financial anxiety is high: 59% are more worried about money than ever, 72% pay closer attention to price and 60% have cut unnecessary spending. Online's share of spending slipped to 51% from 53%, while 48% avoid brands that miss basic digital expectations and 41% regularly abandon purchases after a frustrating online experience.
items.relevance: Consumers are using AI to shortlist but still lean on people and familiar brands to decide, and they are growing wary of paid placement in search. For OOH sellers, that supports the case for fame and trust built in public space, which reaches shoppers before the algorithm does and carries none of the suspicion attached to sponsored results.

pitch.line: 53% of shoppers in 17 countries worry that commercial interests could bias AI shopping tools, and 55% say sponsored results make the best products harder to find (VML Future Shopper 2026).

chart.title: What shoppers say about AI and search, 2026

bars.label: Sponsored results hide the best products

items.headline: Wellness is now a $2.7trn market, and its biggest spenders want proof rather than promises, McKinsey finds
items.dek: A survey of more than 10,000 consumers in four countries shows effectiveness ranking alongside price, while a third of new US packaged goods now carry a health claim.
items.source: McKinsey & Company, Future of Wellness 2027, via NutraIngredients

figures.label: US packaged-goods launches with a wellness claim, Jan–Sep 2026 (24% in 2021)
Share of wellness consumers driving 55% of spending

keyPoints: High-spending wellness consumers were 11 points more likely to say they would buy a longevity product when shown evidence that it works.
In the US, consumers now rate effectiveness as highly as price when choosing wellness products, and the biggest spenders put effectiveness and quality ahead of cost.
Two groups, 'maximalist optimisers' and 'confident enthusiasts', make up 35% of wellness consumers but 55% of spending.
A third of US packaged-goods launches to September 2026 carried at least one health or wellness claim, up from 24% in 2021.
Advice still comes from people: US respondents cite friends and family (35%) and healthcare practitioners (30%) far ahead of AI chatbots (8%).
body: McKinsey's Future of Wellness 2027 research, based on more than 10,000 consumers in the US, UK, Germany and China, values the global wellness market at $2.7trn, including more than $700bn in the US; the firm notes the figure is not directly comparable with its earlier $2trn estimate because the scope has changed. About 40% of consumers report unmet needs, notably in longevity, mental health and mobility.

The defining shift is a demand for evidence. US consumers now weigh effectiveness equally with price, and among the heaviest spenders clear ingredient labelling is one of the five most important considerations for supplements and over-the-counter products. Habits are changing too: among GLP-1 users, 35% have increased their protein intake and 18% have started strength training; 18% of respondents practise health-optimising 'biohacking', rising to 28% of Gen Z; and the share of baby boomers prioritising wellness rose 11 points to 49%.
items.relevance: Wellness brands face buyers who want proof, so claims backed by evidence and clear labelling should anchor creative. Trusted, high-reach channels and in-store presence suit a category where friends, family and practitioners still drive decisions far more than chatbots.

pitch.line: High-spending wellness consumers were 11 points more likely to say they would buy a longevity product when shown evidence that it works (McKinsey Future of Wellness 2027).

chart.title: Where US consumers get advice on wellness purchases

items.headline: A brand that outsells its rival by 25% gets a thirteenth of the AI mentions, Havas Market finds in Latin America
items.dek: Analysing 12,000 answers from eight AI assistants in seven markets, Havas Market finds chatbot visibility bears little relation to real sales, store counts or even whether a brand still exists.
items.source: Havas Market, Lo que dice la IA, via Adlatina

figures.label: Fewer mentions for a brand selling 25% more than its rival

keyPoints: One brand that sells 25% more than its rival is mentioned 13 times less often by AI assistants.
In Argentina, a supermarket chain with 35 stores gets more AI mentions than one with 1,016; in Chile, a company with just over 4% of stores takes almost one mention in four.
In Colombia, the top-selling chain holds more than a quarter of sales among six big groups but fewer than one mention in six.

Assistants disagree and age badly: a carmaker that left Mexico in November 2025 was still being recommended nine months later, and a Costa Rican telecoms firm renamed in 2022 still appeared under its old name 66 times.
body: Havas Market's seven-part series 'Lo que dice la IA' ('What the AI says') put the same questions to eight assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity, DeepSeek, Meta AI, Google AI Overviews and AI Mode) and analysed more than 12,000 responses covering over 140 brands, using a brand-insights tool built by CSA and Havas Market. Mentions were then compared with real sales, store counts and subscriber data across markets including Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Peru, Costa Rica and Mexico.

The gaps are large and inconsistent. Leaders with dominant sales or store networks can be marginal in AI answers, while smaller players are over-represented; in Peru, the most-mentioned chain appears in almost half of one assistant's answers and under 5% of another's. Havas Market concludes that visibility depends on how much information exists about a company and how easily AI can read it. The findings land as ChatGPT Ads expanded to 14 more Latin American markets on 21 October.
items.relevance: AI visibility tracks how much readable information exists about a brand, not market share, so category leaders can be invisible in the answers shoppers increasingly consult. Brands should audit what assistants say about them before buying ads inside them; for real-world media, sustained public fame and press coverage feed the very sources AI draws on.

pitch.line: In Latin America, a brand that sells 25% more than its rival is mentioned 13 times less often by AI assistants (Havas Market, 12,000+ answers from eight assistants).

items.headline: Six in ten American holiday shoppers expect trade-offs, and 72% call Black Friday more hype than savings
items.dek: The Harris Poll's Holiday Edit finds families protecting meaningful gifts and gatherings while cutting treats for themselves, amid deep scepticism about discounts.
items.source: The Harris Poll, The Holiday Edit 2026, via FingerLakes1

figures.label: Say Black Friday and Cyber Monday are more hype than savings
Say sales aren't as good as they used to be
Would cut gifts for themselves first

keyPoints: 72% of US holiday shoppers say Black Friday and Cyber Monday are more hype than genuine savings, and 79% say discounts aren't as good as they used to be.
59% expect financial trade-offs: 32% will scale back and 14% will lean on credit, instalments or savings.
Under pressure, 69% would protect meaningful gifts, 66% gatherings and shared meals and 65% gifts for children; gifts for themselves are the first cut (56%).
Togetherness matters: 30% would rather spend on being together than on gifts, and 76% say traditions keep them grounded.
Tactics are thrifty: 59% will use loyalty points, 56% will wait for promotions and 52% will give to fewer people.
body: The Harris Poll surveyed 1,906 US adults who expected to buy a gift, between 8 and 13 October 2026. Almost six in ten expect to make trade-offs this season, with a third planning to scale back and 14% expecting to rely on credit, instalment payments or savings; 35% said they could celebrate as they wished.

Shoppers are prioritising emotional value. If budgets tighten, meaningful gifts, gatherings and presents for children are protected, while self-gifting goes first. A quarter are spending more on gatherings, and gift cards or cash together are the top preference (34%), with shared experiences the leading single choice (19%). Scepticism about promotions runs high, which the authors note reflects expectations rather than completed purchases.
items.relevance: Value-hunting shoppers who distrust headline discounts respond to credibility and meaning more than another 'up to 70% off'. Retailers can use broad-reach media to frame gatherings, children and shared moments, and keep price claims specific and believable.

pitch.line: 72% of US holiday shoppers say Black Friday and Cyber Monday are more hype than genuine savings (The Harris Poll, 1,906 adults).

chart.title: What US shoppers would protect if budgets tighten

items.headline: American children see almost 4,000 food ads a year on their devices, mostly for junk, a screen-recording study finds
items.dek: Researchers who recorded the screens of more than 1,000 young people found teenagers exposed to over 10,000 food messages a year, 83% of them on social media.
items.source: University of Illinois Chicago, study in JAMA Pediatrics, via Food Dive

figures.label: Food marketing messages seen per young person a year
Non-restaurant foods marketed that were unhealthy

keyPoints: About 83% of the food marketing US children and teens see on their devices comes through social media, with TikTok and YouTube together accounting for more than half.
Teenagers aged 13–17 see more than 10,000 food marketing messages a year; children aged 8–12 close to 1,500.
Fast food (28.8%), sweets (20.4%) and drinks (20.1%) dominate exposure.
About 92% of non-restaurant foods marketed were unhealthy under PAHO nutrient standards, and almost half came from companies in the industry's self-regulatory children's pledge.
body: Led by Lisa Powell, director of the Food Policy Research Program at the University of Illinois Chicago, the study used screen recordings of more than 1,000 children aged 8 to 17 during 30 minutes of normal device use. The authors describe it as the first US study of young people's exposure to food advertising across digital platforms.

Social media carried most exposure, followed by gaming (14%) and web browsing (3.5%). Almost half of the products came from members of the Children's Food and Beverage Advertising Initiative, the industry's voluntary code, which suggests current self-regulation does little to limit what children actually see online.
items.relevance: Policymakers looking at children and food advertising now have measured evidence that exposure is concentrated on personal devices and social platforms. Food and drink brands should expect scrutiny of social and creator activity, and should keep their media mix demonstrably responsible across every channel.

pitch.line: About 83% of the food marketing US children and teens see on their devices comes through social media, with TikTok and YouTube over half (JAMA Pediatrics, 1,000+ young people).

study.by: University of Illinois Chicago (Food Policy Research Program)

chart.title: Food marketing seen by US young people, by category

items.headline: 82% of American shoppers will put private labels in their holiday baskets, Daymon finds
items.dek: Retailers' own brands have become a reason to choose a store, with 71% of shoppers saying private labels decide where they shop.
items.source: Daymon (Advantage Solutions), Holiday 2026 Private Brand Intelligence Report, via GlobeNewswire

figures.label: Plan to buy private brands this holiday
Shop at certain retailers because of their private brands
Expect to spend the same or more on holiday groceries

keyPoints: 71% of US household shoppers say they shop at certain retailers because of their private brands.
82% plan to buy private brands this holiday season, and 87% expect to spend the same or more on holiday groceries.
Younger hosts are stepping up: 52% of Gen Z plan to host Thanksgiving and 53% of millennials plan to host Christmas.
77% plan to buy seasonal flavours, and 69% try to balance healthy choices with indulgence.
body: Daymon, the private-brands unit of Advantage Solutions, based its Holiday 2026 Private Brand Intelligence Report on two national surveys of US adults who shop for their households, with more than 2,000 responses combined. It has produced the report independently since 2018.

The findings show store brands moving from budget fallback to destination: seven in ten shoppers say private labels influence where they shop, and more than eight in ten will buy them over the holidays. Grocery budgets are holding up, with nearly nine in ten planning to spend at least as much as last year, and generational change is shifting who hosts the big meals.
items.relevance: As retailers' own brands become reasons to visit, retailers have more to promote in their own right and more reason to fund store-led campaigns. For media sellers, private-label launches and seasonal ranges are a growing pool of brand-building demand near the store.

pitch.line: 71% of US household shoppers say they choose certain retailers because of their private brands (Daymon, 2,000+ responses).

items.headline: AI assistants have cited impostor sites for one Fortune 500 company in six, often as the official source
items.dek: Scrunch finds that many AI sessions never touch the open web, and that when they do cite sources, fake brand sites slip through for 17% of America's largest companies.
items.source: Scrunch (ScrunchLabs and Sitecore), via GlobeNewswire

figures.label: Fortune 500 companies with an impostor site cited in AI answers
Answers citing a known impostor that present it as official
AI sessions with no open-web search or click
Traditional search sessions that stay self-contained

keyPoints: 17% of Fortune 500 companies have had an impostor website cited in AI answers.
In three of every four answers citing a known impostor, the assistant presented it as the brand's official source.
Scrunch estimates AI assistants deliver more than a million answers a year citing sites that impersonate real brands.
More than 40% of AI sessions involved neither a prior open-web search nor a click out, against 21.5% of traditional search sessions.
body: Scrunch's impostor study examined how ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode and Microsoft Copilot cite sources for Fortune 500 brands. One company in six had an impostor site cited, and the assistants usually framed those sites as official. Scrunch, which sells AI-visibility software, published the findings alongside a new citation-optimisation product.

A companion analysis with Sitecore, 'The New Shape of Search', found that more than 40% of AI sessions stay entirely within the assistant, roughly double the share of self-contained traditional search sessions. The releases do not detail sample sizes or methodology.
items.relevance: As more brand discovery happens inside AI answers, brands lose control over which sources speak for them, including outright fakes. Strong, consistent owned and earned signals matter more, and so do trusted, verifiable brand presences in the physical world.

pitch.line: 17% of Fortune 500 companies have had an impostor website cited in AI answers, presented as the official source three times in four (Scrunch).

items.headline: Supermarkets take the top four places in System1's Christmas ad rankings, with eight ads on a maximum 5.9 stars
items.dek: Morrisons and Sainsbury's lead the early leaderboard, and only 0.3 stars separate first from twelfth in an unusually strong festive field.
items.source: System1, Test Your Ad, via Advanced Television

figures.label: Top-12 Christmas ads on the maximum 5.9 stars
Gap between first and twelfth place

keyPoints: Eight of the UK's top 12 Christmas ads score System1's maximum 5.9 stars, and supermarkets hold the top four places.
Morrisons ('Made Just Right') and Sainsbury's ('Big Delivery') lead on 5.9 stars and a 1.68 Spike score, ahead of M&S and Aldi.
Coca-Cola's AI-made 'Holidays Are Coming' scores 5.7 stars with a strong 1.66 Spike.
Waitrose has the lowest star rating in the top 12 (5.6) but one of the highest Spike scores (1.65); the National Lottery scores 5.9 stars but the lowest Spike (0.98).
body: System1's early leaderboard, drawn from its Test Your Ad platform as of 12 November, shows an exceptionally crowded top tier: Morrisons, Sainsbury's, M&S, Aldi, Thatchers, Disney, Barbour (with Wallace & Gromit) and the National Lottery all reach the maximum 5.9 stars. Coca-Cola, Lidl and Tesco follow on 5.7 and Waitrose on 5.6.

Stars predict long-term brand growth, while Spike measures short-term sales impact, largely driven by how quickly viewers recognise the brand. The split matters: Waitrose's lower star score hides strong branding, while the National Lottery's emotional film carries weaker short-term branding. Supermarkets take seven of the 12 places.
items.relevance: Christmas creative is converging on emotional, well-branded storytelling, so distinctiveness and fast brand recognition separate the winners. Advertisers extending festive films into OOH should carry the brand cues that drive Spike, since OOH audiences give each frame only seconds.

pitch.line: Eight of the UK's top 12 Christmas ads of 2026 score System1's maximum 5.9 stars, and supermarkets hold the top four places (System1).

chart.title: Short-term sales potential (Spike) of leading UK Christmas ads, 2026

items.headline: AI-referred traffic to French retailers has quadrupled in a year, and nearly nine visits in ten land on product pages
items.dek: Valiuz's GEO barometer across 12 retailers shows visits from generative engines equal to 6.4% of search traffic, arriving later in the funnel but browsing less.
items.source: Valiuz, GEO barometer, via CB News

figures.label: Growth in GEO traffic over 12 months
Growth since the previous edition (to 30 June)
GEO traffic as a share of SEO traffic
GEO sessions starting on a product page (60.5% for others)

keyPoints: AI-referred visits to 12 big French retailers' sites quadrupled (×4.03) between September 2025 and September 2026.
GEO traffic grew 49% in the quarter since the previous barometer and now equals 6.4% of organic search traffic on average, above 10% at some retailers.
87.7% of GEO sessions start on a product page, against 60.5% for other sessions.
GEO visitors view 3.36 pages per session against 3.96 site-wide, a 15.2% gap.
body: Valiuz, the retail-media sales house, tracks about 5 million online visits a year across retailers including Auchan, Boulanger, Decathlon, Electro Dépôt, Kiabi, Leroy Merlin and Saint-Maclou for its quarterly generative engine optimisation (GEO) barometer. Cumulative traffic from AI engines has risen about fourfold in a year.

The pattern suggests shoppers arrive from AI with a decision largely made: most land directly on product pages and browse fewer pages than other visitors. Valiuz's Amandine Launois says AI now shapes purchase decisions before shoppers reach the site, and warns that current measurement captures only the visible tip of the iceberg.
items.relevance: AI assistants are compressing the path to purchase, so brands need to be chosen before the click. Retailers and brands should track AI-referred traffic separately and invest in the awareness that gets them named in the first place, where OOH and other mass media still do the heavy lifting.

pitch.line: AI-referred visits to 12 big French retailers' sites quadrupled in a year, and 87.7% start on a product page (Valiuz GEO barometer).

study.sample: About 5 million visits to 12 retailers' sites

chart.title: Sessions that start on a product page

items.headline: Two agencies in three are being asked to cut fees because clients expect AI to make the work cheaper
items.dek: A survey of 300 agency and consultancy bosses by Furious and OpinionWay finds AI reshaping pricing faster than processes, with almost half unable to count the tools a project uses.
items.source: Furious and OpinionWay, via Engage

figures.label: Asked by clients to cut rates because of AI
Expect AI to transform the business model significantly
Openly tell clients how they use AI
Can't say how many AI tools a project needs

keyPoints: 66% of agency and consultancy leaders have been asked by clients to lower rates because AI is expected to cut production costs; for 15% such requests are now routine.
53% expect AI to change the sector's business model significantly and 31% radically.
96% claim a framework for AI use, yet 47% cannot say how many tools a project needs; those who can average 5.8.
Within three years, simple content drafting (46%), data analysis (43%) and document monitoring (41%) are expected to be mostly AI-run.
body: Furious, a project and profitability platform for agencies and consultancies, surveyed 300 executives with OpinionWay. Clients are already pricing in AI: two-thirds of firms have faced requests for lower rates on the assumption that production is cheaper, though 44% say AI enriches client relationships and 62% are open about how they use it.

Governance lags adoption. Almost all respondents say they have a framework, but nearly half cannot tally the tools used on a project. Most (66%) expect AI and human skills to be fully integrated within three years, redefining roles, and only 7% expect AI to become the main productive resource.
items.relevance: Fee pressure from AI will push agencies to price on outcomes and ideas rather than hours, and clients will expect production savings to show up. Marketers should agree how AI savings are shared and insist on transparency over which tools and data touch their brand.

pitch.line: 66% of agency and consultancy leaders have been asked by clients to lower rates because AI is expected to cut production costs (Furious/OpinionWay, 300 executives).

items.headline: Only half of Brazilians plan to shop on Black Friday, down 37 points since 2023, as debt bites
items.dek: The CNDL/SPC Brasil survey finds planned spending down to R$1,053, PIX the favourite way to pay and almost two-thirds of buyers afraid of fraud.
items.source: CNDL and SPC Brasil, Black Friday 2026 survey (with Offerwise), via Varejo S.A.

figures.label: Plan to buy on Black Friday (−37 pts vs 2023)

keyPoints: Only 51% of Brazilians in state capitals plan to buy on Black Friday 2026, down 37 points since 2023; 31% are undecided.
Among non-buyers, 26% cite lack of money, 16% debt and 15% unemployment; 57% of buyers are still paying off other instalment purchases.
Average planned spend is R$1,053 on about three products, with an expected average discount of 42%.
81% plan to buy online (50% on international sites or apps), 46% in physical stores; 63% will pay by PIX.
Clothing and accessories lead (41%), followed by electronics (32%), beauty and home goods (28% each).
body: CNDL and SPC Brasil surveyed consumers in Brazil's 27 state capitals with Offerwise between 7 and 19 October: 1,133 people to gauge intent, then 601 intending buyers. Seven in ten buyers want products they need at lower prices, 37% will start Christmas shopping early and 69% are delaying some purchase until the event.

Price comparison and free shipping (41% each) are the main reasons to choose a store, ahead of known brands (29%). Almost half will pay in instalments, averaging six, and 65% fear fraud such as card cloning. Timing is concentrated: 42% will shop during Black Friday week and 28% from early November.
items.relevance: Brazil's Black Friday is shrinking and fragmenting into a cautious, comparison-driven month. Retailers and brands need credible offers and trust signals, with early awareness to make the shortlist before price comparison takes over.

pitch.line: Only 51% of Brazilians in state capitals plan to buy on Black Friday 2026, down 37 points since 2023 (CNDL/SPC Brasil).

chart.title: What Brazilian Black Friday buyers plan to purchase

items.headline: Australian consumer sentiment falls to a four-year low as the year's fifth rate rise bites
items.dek: The Westpac-Melbourne Institute index dropped 2.7% to 78.2 in November, its third monthly fall and nearly a quarter below a year ago, just as retailers enter peak season.
items.source: Westpac-Melbourne Institute Index of Consumer Sentiment, via IndexBox (citing Reuters)

figures.label: RBA cash rate after fifth rise of 2026

keyPoints: Australian consumer sentiment fell to 78.2 in November 2026, the weakest reading in four years and nearly 25% below a year earlier.
It is the third monthly decline in a row, after falls of 5.2% in September and 4.7% in October.
The 12-month economic outlook sub-index fell 10.2%, and 'good time to buy a major household item' fell 3.7%.
The Reserve Bank has raised rates five times this year, to 4.85%, an 18-year high.
body: The Westpac-Melbourne Institute index slid 2.7% in November as the Reserve Bank of Australia continued tightening to fight inflation, taking the cash rate to its highest in 18 years. Pessimists far outnumber optimists, and Westpac's Matthew Hassan said households were bracing for further increases.

The weakest components were forward-looking: expectations for the economy over the next year dropped by a tenth, and willingness to make big household purchases also fell. The reading lands just before Black Friday and Christmas, for which retailers had forecast record spending.
items.relevance: Australian shoppers are entering peak season anxious and selective, which favours retailers with clear value and trusted brands. Advertisers should keep visibility through the slowdown rather than go dark, while tightening offers and timing around pay cycles and key sale days.

pitch.line: Australian consumer sentiment fell to 78.2 in November 2026, a four-year low and nearly 25% below a year earlier (Westpac-Melbourne Institute).

chart.title: Monthly change in Australian consumer sentiment, 2026

items.headline: WOO warns of a domino effect as OOH bans spread, with Hungary stripping Budapest of almost every billboard
items.dek: Reporting on its Warsaw regulation session, the World Out of Home Organization mapped restrictions from Amsterdam to Rio and set out a defence playbook, as Hungary's new law threatens some 300 media owners.
items.source: WOO (World Out of Home Organization), Warsaw 2026 regulation session

figures.label: Hungarian media owners expected to fail
Budapest's share of Hungary's OOH market
Hungarian advertisers planning to cut OOH budgets

keyPoints: Hungary's national law, in force since 1 October, requires sites to come down by 31 December: all billboards in Budapest and about 90% elsewhere, with building wraps and freestanding citylights banned nationwide.

About 300 Hungarian media owners are expected to fail, putting roughly 1,200 jobs and HUF5bn a year in tax revenue at risk; 49% of advertisers plan to cut OOH budgets and 77% to shift spend to social media.

Restrictions are spreading: Amsterdam's citywide meat and fossil-fuel ban took effect on 1 May, Bristol's fast-fashion ban in September, Poland's parliament voted a total alcohol-ad ban on 8 October and Rio has removed betting ads.
WOO vice-president Kai-Marcus Thäsler says bans are rarely about revenue (meat is 0.1% of Amsterdam's OOH market) but about precedent, and are shifting from the message to the medium itself.
WOO is launching a Global Policy Radar and Policy Academy, urging members to act early, use evidence, build alliances, offer self-regulation and protect the medium's reputation.
body: The session at WOO's Central European Forum in Warsaw brought together Thäsler, who also runs Germany's FAW, Tamás Bauer of IK Outdoor and the Hungarian Advertising Association, Paweł Orłowski of Synergic in Poland and Andreas Allerstorfer of Austria's AWS. Thäsler identified six ways to restrict a medium (ban the product, the format, the pixels, the place, the data, or tax it) and four trends: category creep, courts backing cities, a shift from message to medium and global spread.

Hungary is the starkest case. Bauer expects only Publimont and JCDecaux to survive, with remaining digital screens limited to static spots of at least 20 seconds and switched off from 10pm to 6am; no impact assessment preceded the law. Courts have cut both ways elsewhere: Lyon's blanket digital ban was struck down and Poland's Constitutional Tribunal ruled removal without compensation unconstitutional. WOO's case for the medium cites low annoyance (10% for OOH against 47% for music streaming, per Havas), a small carbon footprint, safety data and public benefits such as emergency messaging and funding for cities.
items.relevance: Restrictions are moving from individual categories to the medium itself, and one city's rule quickly becomes another's template. Buyers planning European OOH should check category and format rules city by city; owners and associations need evidence-led engagement with cities long before votes are scheduled.

pitch.line: Only 10% of people find OOH annoying, against 38% for linear TV and 47% for music streaming (Havas 2025, cited by WOO).

chart.title: Share of people who find each medium annoying (Havas, 2025)

items.headline: Ocean Outdoor links Piccadilly Lights with Shibuya's giant screens in a reciprocal sales pact with Japan's Hit
items.dek: The exclusive agreement lets each company sell the other's premium inventory at home, taking Ocean's international alliance to 13 countries.
items.source: Ocean Outdoor, company release

figures.label: Screens in Hit's Synchro 7 Shibuya network
UK cities with Ocean DOOH networks

keyPoints: Ocean Outdoor UK and Hit Co. have signed a mutual exclusive agreement under which each becomes the sole sales contact for the other's OOH portfolio in its home market.

Hit's inventory includes Shibuhachi Hit Vision facing Shibuya's Hachiko Square, the seven-screen Synchro 7 Shibuya network and an LED network along Tokyo's Metropolitan Expressway, plus sites in Ikebukuro, Harajuku and Osaka.
Ocean brings Piccadilly Lights (operated for Landsec), the BFI IMAX in Waterloo, The Curve in Leicester Square and DOOH networks in 20 UK cities.
The deal extends Ocean's alliance to Japan; it already covers markets including the US, China, Australia, Spain, Italy, Sweden, the Netherlands and France.
body: The partnership gives international advertisers a single route to two of the world's most photographed screen clusters. Japanese brands can book London landmarks through Hit, and UK and international brands can buy Shibuya and Tokyo inventory through Ocean.
Nick Shaw, chief executive of Ocean Outdoor UK, said the agreement lets global brands extend their presence and widens Ocean's alliance footprint across Japan.
items.relevance: Cross-border alliances between landmark owners make it easier to plan 'global icon' campaigns without a network deal in every market. Media owners with trophy sites should consider reciprocal sales partnerships to capture international budgets.

pitch.line: Ocean Outdoor's international alliance now spans 13 countries after a reciprocal exclusive sales deal with Japan's Hit Co. (Ocean Outdoor).

items.headline: Germany's DOOH Creative Challenge rewards bold, cross-media work but withholds gold for best use of data
items.dek: Borussia Dortmund, Condor and LBS took the top prizes at the IDOOH association's year-end awards, while the jury left two categories without a gold.
items.source: MEEDIA, on the DOOH Creative Challenge 2026 (IDOOH)
keyPoints: Best of DOOH Creation: 'Vorteil BVB' for Borussia Dortmund by denkwerk, drawing attention to deafness.
Best of Crossmedia: 'Auf Streifzug mit Condor', the airline's rebrand, by K3 Agency, dentsu X and M.A.I.S.
Best of Innovative DOOH: 'RINtnerweisheiten' for LBS with rapper RIN, by Huth + Wenzel with OMD Germany, combining social media and OOH.
No gold was awarded for Best Use of Data; the YoungStars gold went to 'Night Safety Screens' for the Heimwegtelefon walk-home helpline.
body: The DOOH Creative Challenge is Germany's annual awards for digital OOH, presented at the autumn conference of the IDOOH industry association. The jury, including Alexander Stotz of Ströer, rewarded work that used the medium boldly or combined it with other media and data, but withheld gold in two categories and said it wanted more from the entries.
The conference also discussed sustainability and energy efficiency, and the YoungStars category for emerging talent focused on social causes.
items.relevance: The winners show German DOOH moving towards cross-media ideas that connect screens with social platforms and brand platforms. The missing data gold is a reminder that data-driven DOOH creative is still rare, an opening for owners and agencies that can show it working.

items.headline: Metads builds a walk-in 3D DOOH cube for Düsseldorf's Christmas market
items.dek: 'Portal 216' wraps visitors in about 100 m² of LED across three walls and the ceiling, with Sephora among the first brands tested.
items.source: Campaign Germany, on Metads

figures.label: Area versus a standard digital ad screen

keyPoints: Metads' 'Portal 216' is a walk-in cube five metres high, wide and deep, taller than a double-decker bus, with LEDs on the ceiling and three walls.
Its roughly 100 m² of LED offers about 50 times the area of a standard digital advertising screen, and all content is in 3D.
Sephora is the only advertiser named so far; its animated perfume bottles and brushes were shown to test customers.
The cube was built and tested in a hall before installation at Düsseldorf's Christmas market.
body: Metads developed the installation with clients as an immersive format for the festive season, turning a DOOH screen into a space visitors step inside rather than look at. The article compares its scale with the Ferris wheel on Burgplatz but does not confirm the exact location or the media owner.

Immersive 3D formats have mostly appeared on building-sized anamorphic screens; a walk-in cube brings the effect to street level, where dwell time is longer and the experience can be filmed and shared.
items.relevance: Experiential DOOH formats at seasonal events give brands content as well as reach. Beauty and luxury brands, in particular, can use immersive 3D to show products at scale where shoppers already gather.

pitch.line: Metads' walk-in 'Portal 216' cube offers about 100 m² of LED, roughly 50 times the area of a standard digital ad screen (Campaign Germany).

items.headline: Network X bets on South Africa's townships, sharing ad revenue with the small businesses that host its billboards
items.dek: The OOH company places sites at taverns, spaza shops, car washes and clinics in a market of up to 22 million people worth an estimated R1trn, and is drawing premium brands.
items.source: Business Day, Spotlight podcast with Network X
keyPoints: Network X places billboards outside township convenience hubs such as taverns, spaza shops, car washes and clinics.
Sales director Jason Steyn argues townships are not poor environments: the market numbers an estimated 15–22 million people worth about R1trn.
Premium brands are investing, including Hennessy, banks, telecoms operators and money-transfer services WorldRemit, MoneyGram and Mukuru.
The company pays the black-owned small businesses that host its sites a percentage of ad revenue, covers their electricity and provides backup power.
body: In a Business Day Spotlight podcast, Steyn set out Network X's strategy of building OOH networks at the places township residents visit every day. The host-partnership model, which shares revenue with site owners and keeps the lights on during power cuts, is designed to differentiate the company and secure sites.
The conversation also covered the resilience of billboard advertising and how AI is changing the sector.
items.relevance: Township retail is one of South Africa's largest and least-served media markets, and proximity formats at daily-errand locations reach it at scale. Financial services, telecoms and FMCG brands chasing growth should treat township OOH as a mainstream buy rather than a niche.

pitch.line: South Africa's township market of 15–22 million people is worth an estimated R1 trillion (Network X, via Business Day).

items.headline: Moving billboards beat a click benchmark by 350% at Advertising Week New York, OAAA's MDMA reports
items.dek: A two-day shadowfencing test pairing branded vehicles with mobile retargeting delivered 408,000 impressions, with retargeting nearly doubling the click rate.
items.source: OOH Today, on OAAA's Moving and Dynamic Media Alliance
keyPoints: A moving-media campaign with mobile retargeting at Advertising Week New York delivered a 0.27% click-through rate, which MDMA says is 350% above the advertising-and-marketing benchmark.
Over 48 hours in Manhattan it generated more than 408,000 impressions and 1,100 clicks.
Retargeting people who had been near the vehicles produced a 0.52% click-through rate, almost double the campaign average and the best of any tactic.
The figures combine moving media and digital activity and are reported by MDMA itself; no third-party measurement is named.
body: The OAAA's Moving and Dynamic Media Alliance ran the activation with participating moving-media operators, using shadowfencing (location-based targeting around the vehicles' routes) and digital retargeting. QR codes on the vehicles offered attendees MDMA's strategic guide to moving and dynamic OOH.
Regis Maher, MDMA chair, reported the results. Because the campaign blended vehicle media with digital follow-up, it shows the value of the combination rather than isolating the vehicles' own effect.
items.relevance: Mobile OOH paired with location-based retargeting can turn street exposure into measurable digital response. Buyers should ask for clean splits between OOH-exposed and unexposed audiences before relying on such benchmarks.

pitch.line: A moving-billboard campaign with mobile retargeting at Advertising Week New York delivered a 0.27% click-through rate, 350% above the advertising-and-marketing benchmark (OAAA MDMA).

brief: AI agents are reaching the shop faster than the checkout: HUMAN Security says agent traffic to websites grew 157.5% in October, mostly product research, while 43% of Americans now let AI shape a final purchase, Alvarez & Marsal finds.

Peak season is about value and proof: Singles Day grew just 3.7% to CNY1.68trn, Australians plan a record A$7.2bn Black Friday weekend, and 38% of Brazilians are still undecided because they doubt the discounts.

In real-world media, Lamar bought more than 2,250 Newman Outdoor faces to lead North Dakota, FIRB cleared I Squared's oOh!media takeover, and Rotana Signs brought CESP-validated audience measurement to Saudi OOH.
Diary: bids for co-branding rights at 12 Delhi Metro stations close on 16 November, oOh!media's scheme goes to court on 18 November and Schiphol's €426m advertising tender closes on 20 November.

numberOfDay.line: AI-agent traffic to websites grew 157.5% in October 2026 alone, with Meta and OpenAI sending 89% of agent requests (HUMAN Security).

steal.title: Sell the late shift
steal.text: StreetMetrics data shows that late on Friday and Saturday nights a billboard's audience reaches further out, with visitors from 10–50 miles away making up about a fifth more of passes in all 12 US markets measured. The idea worth stealing: package weekend 10pm–midnight digital slots as a 'night-out' audience for restaurants, venues, ride-hailing and late-opening retail.

items.headline: AI-agent traffic to websites jumps 157% in a month, and Meta and OpenAI now send nine requests in ten
items.dek: HUMAN Security's October data shows AI shopping and browsing agents multiplying eightfold since August, overwhelmingly landing on product and search pages rather than checkouts.
items.source: HUMAN Security, agentic traffic report (October 2026), via PPC Land

figures.label: Agentic traffic growth, October vs September
Share of agent requests from Meta and OpenAI
Agent requests landing on product and search pages
Share of agent traffic hitting e-commerce sites

keyPoints: Requests from AI agents to the sites HUMAN protects grew 157.5% between September and October 2026, roughly eight times the August level.
Two companies dominate: Meta and OpenAI generated 89% of agent requests, with Meta's Muse alone at 59% and OpenAI's three agent products at about 30%.
Perplexity's Comet collapsed from 41% of agent traffic in August to 3.6%; Anthropic's Claude Chrome extension held 3.5%, Google's agent 0.8%.
Agents mostly browse: 85.2% of requests hit product and search pages and only 1.9% checkout and payment, with e-commerce taking 59.9% of the traffic, travel 19.3% and media 19.1%.
body: HUMAN Security's Satori threat-intelligence team measured agentic requests across the applications protected by its Sightline platform during October 2026, identifying agents through behavioural signals, user-agent attribution and publisher integrations. The figures count requests rather than people or sessions and are HUMAN's own, unaudited data.

The month's growth was explosive: agent traffic rose 157.5% on September and is about eight times August's volume. The market has also consolidated fast. Meta's Muse agent accounted for 59% of requests and OpenAI's ChatGPT Agent, Codex Browser and Codex Chrome extension for about 30% between them, while Perplexity's Comet, which led in August with 41%, fell to 3.6%. Most of the activity is research rather than buying: 85.2% of requests landed on product and search pages and 1.9% on checkout and payment, although HUMAN reports a 117% month-on-month rise in checkout request volume, a figure PPC Land notes the published shares do not fully support.
items.relevance: AI agents are becoming a real audience for retail and travel brands, but they are still researching rather than buying, which means the brand a shopper asks for by name still matters. For OOH sellers, this strengthens the case for fame-building media that puts a brand in the prompt before an agent starts comparing options.

pitch.line: AI-agent traffic to websites grew 157.5% in October 2026 alone, and 85% of it was product research rather than checkout (HUMAN Security).

chart.title: Share of AI-agent requests by agent, October 2026

items.headline: Six in ten corporate communicators now prefer silence on divisive issues, Ipsos's Reputation Council finds
items.dek: Senior communications chiefs at some of the world's largest companies say politics shapes when they speak, and a fifth have deliberately played down real ESG progress.
items.source: Ipsos, Reputation Council Report 2026, via MediaNews4U

figures.label: Weigh political factors before speaking up

keyPoints: 84% of senior communications leaders say their organisations weigh political factors before deciding whether to speak up, and 61% prefer silence on divisive subjects even when they could take an authentic position.
35% say their organisation stayed quiet in the past year on issues it would once have addressed, and 22% deliberately under-communicated credible ESG progress.
Only 17% agree that such 'strategic silence' amounts to corporate cowardice; 46% see populism as a material risk.
AI has gone mainstream in corporate affairs: 76% report meaningful use, up from 43% in 2025, yet only 12% think existing ethics policies are adequate.
body: The 19th edition of the Ipsos Reputation Council, titled 'Life After Predictability', is based on 200 one-to-one interviews with senior communications and corporate-affairs leaders at large organisations. Its central finding is that volatility is now treated as permanent, and that many companies have responded by speaking less.

Political calculation has become routine: 84% factor it into decisions about speaking out, 61% would rather stay silent on divisive topics, and 35% have recently held back on issues they would previously have addressed. ESG communication is narrowing too: 61% say it has become more targeted and 22% admit under-selling real progress. Meanwhile 76% now use AI meaningfully, against 43% a year ago, but only 12% believe their ethics policies are fit for it. The full report is available on request from Ipsos.
items.relevance: As corporate voices retreat from public debate, brands' messaging is becoming more cautious and more product-led. Public, broadcast-style media such as OOH carry a reputational weight that targeted channels do not, so planners should brief creative that is confident without being divisive.

pitch.line: 61% of senior corporate communicators now prefer to stay silent on divisive issues, even when they could take an authentic stance (Ipsos Reputation Council 2026).

study.sample: 200 senior communications and corporate-affairs leaders (one-to-one interviews)

chart.title: Corporate communicators: speaking up in 2026

report.label: Ipsos Reputation Council Report 2026

items.headline: Patients are becoming shoppers: four in ten trust online health advice as much as a doctor's, BCG finds
items.dek: A ten-market survey shows China, India and the UAE leading a shift towards consumer-style healthcare, with millennials the most willing to take an instant AI answer over a wait.
items.source: BCG, The Consumerization of Health Care, via MediaNews4U

figures.label: Indians who rate online health info as reliable as a professional
Global millennials preferring an instant AI or online answer
Higher-income consumers willing to pay out of pocket for wellness products

keyPoints: BCG's Health Care Consumerization Index puts China first (72), India second (66), the UAE third (63) and Brazil fourth (62) of ten markets; Japan is last on 36.
60% of Indian respondents consider online health information as reliable as professional advice, 19 points above the global average, and 61% prefer an instant AI or online answer.
Generations split sharply: 52% of millennials and 47% of Gen Z worldwide prefer an instant AI or online answer, against 25% of baby boomers.

Medicines are being treated like consumer goods: 53% of millennials see them as comparable to everyday products, and 48% of higher-income consumers would pay out of pocket for items such as GLP-1 drugs.
body: BCG surveyed nearly 10,000 consumers in India, China, the US, the UK, Germany, France, Brazil, Japan, Switzerland and the UAE for its report on how patients are reshaping healthcare. Its index scores each market on six measures of consumer-style behaviour, from appetite for control over treatment to expectations of retail-grade convenience.

India stands out alongside China: 78% of Indians want more control over treatment choices, 73% want more control over costs and payment, and 68% expect providers to match retail levels of service. Younger cohorts drive the change globally, with millennials the most willing to accept an instant answer from AI or the web rather than wait for a professional. Income matters too: 48% of higher-income consumers worldwide would pay out of pocket for some health and wellness products, against 31% of lower-income ones.
items.relevance: Health and pharma brands are now marketing to shoppers rather than patients, especially in Asia and the Gulf. That calls for retail-style brand building and trust signals in public spaces, near pharmacies and on commuter routes, as well as online.

pitch.line: 60% of Indian consumers rate online health information as reliable as professional advice, 19 points above the global average (BCG).

study.markets: 10 countries (India, China, US, UK, Germany, France, Brazil, Japan, Switzerland, UAE)

chart.title: BCG Health Care Consumerization Index, 2026

items.headline: Four in five large companies now run AI agents, but only 15% can tie the spending to profit, Genpact finds
items.dek: A survey of more than 2,000 senior executives shows AI now leading 40% of business decisions, while only half of funded AI projects delivered the value expected.
items.source: Genpact, Autonomy in Practice

figures.label: Enterprises with AI agents in production
Have fully tied AI investment to P&L
AI initiatives that delivered expected value
Decisions led or run by AI (double last year)

keyPoints: 79% of large enterprises have AI agents in production, but only 20% use them broadly across functions and only 15% have fully tied AI investment to profit-and-loss outcomes.
Just 49% of AI initiatives funded in the past two years delivered the expected value, and only 9% of companies have completed a significant operating-model change.
AI now leads or runs 40% of decisions, more than double last year, yet humans still decide or audit in at least 87% of cases at every stage.
92% of companies with agents in production kept or grew their workforce.
body: Genpact surveyed more than 2,000 senior executives at companies with revenues from $1bn to over $50bn, across 17 industries and 14 functions, supplemented by interviews. The findings are self-reported.

The study describes a gap between deployment and pay-off. Agents are widespread, but few companies have redesigned their operations around them or linked the spending to the profit line, and only half of funded projects met expectations. Even so, autonomy is rising: AI now leads or fully runs 40% of decisions, with humans firmly in the loop for oversight, and most companies say adoption has not cut headcount.
items.relevance: Marketing departments face the same proof problem as the rest of the business: budgets are moving to AI faster than returns can be shown. Media with established, measurable effects, OOH among them, can position themselves as the accountable part of a plan while AI spending is still being justified.

pitch.line: 79% of large enterprises run AI agents in production, but only 15% have fully tied AI investment to P&L outcomes (Genpact, Autonomy in Practice).

study.sample: 2,000+ senior executives at companies with $1bn–$50bn+ revenue

report.label: Genpact: Autonomy in Practice

items.headline: America's holiday splits by income: the rich plan to spend more, everyone else cuts gifts and decorations
items.dek: Alvarez & Marsal's autumn survey finds overall spending intent at its highest since 2023, but holiday intent sharply negative, with store brands, GLP-1 users and AI advice all reshaping baskets.
items.source: Alvarez & Marsal Consumer and Retail Group, Fall 2026 Consumer Sentiment Survey

figures.label: Net holiday spending intent (about −3% last autumn)
Let AI influence a final purchase at least sometimes (35% before)
Say store brands are more affordable

keyPoints: Net holiday spending intent fell to −14% from about −3% a year ago, even though overall spending intent (+4% net) is the highest since autumn 2023.
The split is by income: higher-income households show +18% net holiday intent, lower-income households −26%, with decorations (−43%) and travel (−36%) hit hardest.
43% now let AI influence their final purchase at least sometimes, up from 35%; 60% of under-45s use AI for shopping against 27% of older consumers.
In-store's lead over online for final purchases has narrowed from 26 points to 15; 26% are switching to cheaper grocers while keeping their brands, up from 16%.
body: Alvarez & Marsal surveyed more than 2,000 nationally representative US adults for its autumn sentiment study. The headline picture is an uneven recovery: overall spending intent has turned positive, led by wealthier households, 63% of which expect to earn more, while lower-income households are net-negative in every category except groceries and pet supplies.

Holiday budgets are where the gap shows most. Higher-income shoppers plan to spend more on meals and treats (+21%) and travel (+17%), while lower-income ones are cutting gifts for themselves (−34%), travel (−36%) and decorations (−43%). About half are waiting for Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Store brands keep gaining credibility, with 69% rating their quality as good or better, and 22% of respondents say they currently take a GLP-1 medication, which the report notes is above national estimates. Shopping is increasingly blended: 39% mix online and in-store, and 35% call that their ideal.
items.relevance: US holiday plans should be segmented by income rather than averaged: premium categories still have growth, while mass brands are fighting own-label and trade-down. With in-store still winning most final purchases, near-store and roadside OOH remains a strong last-mile lever for both groups.

pitch.line: 43% of US consumers now let AI influence their final purchase decision at least sometimes, up from 35% a year ago (Alvarez & Marsal).

study.by: Alvarez & Marsal Consumer and Retail Group

chart.title: US net holiday spending intent by category, lower-income households

report.label: Alvarez & Marsal: Consumer Sentiment Survey, Fall 2026

items.headline: Missing data sends six in ten CTV buyers to another supply path, CIMM finds
items.dek: A study of programmatic connected-TV buyers shows transparency now ranks alongside scale, and that buyers punish inventory that arrives without the signals they need.
items.source: CIMM, Behind the Bidstream: The Signals that Matter, via PPC Land

figures.label: Buyers who shift spend when signals are missing
Say DSPs always apply their required signals
Likely to bid with detailed signals on a verified path
Rank supply-path transparency in their top three

keyPoints: 62% of programmatic CTV buyers move spend to another supply path when required signals are missing; 54% broaden targeting and 46% cut their bids.
Only 8% say their DSP always operationalises their required signals once a campaign is live.
Verification matters most: 88% are likely to bid on detailed signals via a verified path, against 36% for the same signals via an unverified one.
Supply-path transparency (48%) now edges scale and reach (46%) among buyers' top-three priorities.
body: The Coalition for Innovative Media Measurement published the paper, co-sponsored by FreeWheel and OpenX, on 12 November. It combines a survey of 50 qualified programmatic CTV buyers, fielded in May and June 2026, with interviews of 28 senior publisher and platform executives and bid-log analysis from the two sponsors.

Buyers are decisive when data is missing: most redirect spend, many loosen targeting or lower bids, and two-thirds work with the seller to fix the problem. Execution is the weak link, with only 8% saying DSPs always honour the signals they specify. The study's message to sellers is that a verified supply path with rich, consistent signals wins bids; under pacing pressure, though, only 27% of buyers kept their signal requirements unchanged.
items.relevance: The same rules apply to programmatic DOOH: buyers reward inventory that comes with clean, verified data on audience, location and playout. Real-world media owners selling through SSPs should treat signal quality and supply-path transparency as a pricing lever, not a technical detail.

pitch.line: 62% of programmatic CTV buyers shift spend to another supply path when the signals they need are missing (CIMM, Behind the Bidstream).

study.by: CIMM (with FreeWheel and OpenX; survey by Ozona Insights, fielded by OvationMR)
study.sample: 50 programmatic CTV buyers plus 28 executive interviews

chart.title: What CTV buyers do when required signals are missing

items.headline: Billboards draw a wider audience late on Friday and Saturday nights, StreetMetrics data shows
items.dek: Between 10pm and midnight at weekends, viewers from 10 to 50 miles away make up about a fifth more of a board's passes than at other times, across all 12 markets measured.
items.source: OOH Today, Stat of the Week, on StreetMetrics data

figures.label: Extra share of passes from 10–50 miles away, Fri/Sat 10pm–midnight

keyPoints: Late on Friday and Saturday nights, from 10pm to midnight, the audience travelling from 10 to 50 miles away accounts for about 20% more of a board's passes than during the rest of the week.
The pattern held in all 12 measured US markets, in both September and February 2026.
Weekday evenings and Saturday midday show no such shift: on most nights a board's late audience is local.
The measure is share of viewable passes, not reach.
body: OOH Today's weekly statistic, powered by StreetMetrics viewable board-pass data, compared the origin of passing audiences by daypart across 12 US markets in September and February. Late weekend nights stood out: the share of passes made by people from 10 to 50 miles away rose by about a fifth compared with the rest of the week.

The implication is mainly for digital inventory, which can be scheduled by the hour. Restaurants, entertainment venues, ride-hailing services and late-opening retailers trying to reach suburban households may find these two hours a better fit than a weekday schedule suggests. The source does not give the number of boards or passes measured.
items.relevance: This is a practical dayparting argument for digital OOH: weekend late slots reach visitors as well as locals, which suits leisure, hospitality and mobility brands. Sellers can package Friday and Saturday 10pm–midnight as a distinct 'night-out' audience.

pitch.line: On Friday and Saturday nights after 10pm, visitors from 10–50 miles away make up about 20% more of a billboard's audience than the rest of the week, in all 12 US markets measured (StreetMetrics).

items.headline: Half of French shoppers now let a brand's responsibility sway them, and want the proof in store
items.dek: Valiuz's Sustainable Brands study finds a 12-point jump in a year, led by under-37s, with health overtaking the planet as the reason people change their habits.
items.source: e-marketing.fr, on Valiuz's Sustainable Brands study (4th edition)

figures.label: Strongly influenced by a brand's responsibility (+12 pts)
Would pay more for a committed brand
Expect brand commitments on in-store digital screens
Believe companies communicate honestly (+11 pts in two years)

keyPoints: 50% of French consumers say a brand's responsible character strongly influences them, up 12 points in a year, rising to 62% among under-37s.
Health has become the main driver of more responsible habits (43%), while protecting the planet fell 15 points to 37%.
66% expect to see brand commitments on in-store digital screens, and stores (37%) beat e-commerce (28%) as the preferred place to learn about them.
Trust is recovering: 39% think companies communicate honestly, up 11 points in two years, but 75% want claims backed by concrete proof.
body: The fourth edition of the Sustainable Brands study by Valiuz, the retail-data company, shows responsibility moving from niche to mainstream in France. Purchasing power (44%) still tops household concerns, followed by health (37%) and security (31%), but 57% say they would spend more with a committed brand and the share who find such brands hard to identify has fallen from 72% in 2024 to 58%.

The study points to the shop floor as the place to make the case. Consumers want origin, composition and anti-waste credentials for food (71%) and durability and repairability for non-food (72%), and 76% say it matters that retailers highlight such efforts in store. Three-quarters of French people have bought second-hand or refurbished goods, rising to 89% of under-37s. The article does not give the sample size.
items.relevance: French shoppers want sustainability claims proved at the point of purchase, and two-thirds expect to see them on in-store screens. That gives retail-media and DOOH sellers a ready brief: evidence-led messages near the shelf, not abstract purpose campaigns.

pitch.line: 66% of French consumers expect brands' responsibility commitments to be shown on in-store digital screens (Valiuz, Sustainable Brands 2026).

items.headline: In a crisis, the French still turn to live television and trust scientists, CSA and Havas find
items.dek: Two-thirds rely on TV when risks strike, but only one in eight turns to creators, rising to more than a quarter of 18–24-year-olds.
items.source: e-marketing.fr, on CSA Research and Havas Media Network's Consumer Lab

figures.label: Use TV (live and streaming) in a crisis
Prefer scientists and technical experts as sources
Feel directly concerned by a major risk

keyPoints: 68% of French people turn to television in a crisis (62% to live TV), against 36% for live radio and 30% for newspaper websites.
Scientists and technical experts (52%) and front-line professionals (51%) are the preferred sources; creators and influencers draw 12%, rising to 27% among 18–24-year-olds.
75% feel directly concerned by at least one major risk, from extreme weather to health threats and cyberattacks.
Gaps are wide: 85% of over-65s follow major-risk news against 64% of 18–24s, and 83% in the Paris area against 62% in the north.
body: CSA Research and the Consumer Lab of Havas Media Network surveyed 1,010 people in France between 14 and 21 September 2026 on how they follow news about risks and crises. Nine in ten follow the news regularly, and natural events such as heatwaves and floods (57%) are the most-followed topic, ahead of wars (50%) and crime (49%).

When something goes wrong, legacy media regain their pull: television leads with 68%, while news pure players and YouTube each reach 14%. Trust scores are highest for front-line professionals (8.3 out of 10) and scientists (8.2), with journalists on 7. The age and regional gaps suggest that a single national plan no longer reaches everyone equally.
items.relevance: Trusted, broad-reach environments still matter when audiences feel uncertain, and expert voices carry more weight than influencers for most adults. Brands in insurance, energy and health can borrow that authority in public, high-visibility media rather than relying on creator content alone.

pitch.line: 68% of French people turn to television in a crisis, while only 12% look to creators and influencers (CSA Research and Havas Media Network).

study.by: CSA Research and Havas Media Network Consumer Lab

chart.title: Media used by the French in a crisis

items.headline: Nearly four in ten Brazilians are still undecided about Black Friday, and doubt the discounts
items.dek: A TOTVS and Opinion Box survey finds marketplaces dominating discovery and purchase, while social networks inspire but rarely close the sale.
items.source: BP Money, on a TOTVS and Opinion Box survey

figures.label: Say discounts are much better than the rest of the year
Use social networks for discovery / to buy
Trust an influencer when content is labelled as paid

keyPoints: 38% of Brazilians have not decided whether to buy on Black Friday 2026, although 53% plan to take advantage of it and 69% follow the promotions.
Only 22% think the discounts are much better than the rest of the year; among those ruling out a purchase, 33% see no real price advantage and 26% doubt advertised prices.
Marketplaces lead every stage (45% discovery, 43% research, 38% purchase); social networks inspire 35% but close only 5% of purchases.
Specialists' product videos (46%) and consumer reviews (42%) are trusted far more than influencers in labelled paid posts (20%).
body: TOTVS, the Brazilian software group, and Opinion Box surveyed 2,109 Brazilians aged 18 and over across all regions and social classes between 10 and 22 October 2026 (margin of error 2.1 points). The picture is of a planned but sceptical shopper: 41% start planning at least a month ahead and 51% already know what they want when the day arrives.

Discounts (55%), free delivery (53%) and interest-free instalments (37%) are the conditions that convert. Scepticism about price claims is the main barrier, and trust sits with independent expertise and peer reviews rather than paid creators.
items.relevance: In Brazil, Black Friday demand is there but credibility is not. Brands should lead with clear, verifiable prices and conditions, and use broad public media to reassure undecided shoppers before they reach the marketplace where the sale is closed.

pitch.line: 38% of Brazilians are still undecided about Black Friday 2026, and only 22% think the discounts are much better than the rest of the year (TOTVS and Opinion Box).

chart.title: Where Brazilians discover and buy on Black Friday

items.headline: Visitors drawn to the Middle East want luxury and culture far more than other travellers, ATM report finds
items.dek: Arabian Travel Market's 2026 trends report, built with Tourism Economics, shows the region attracting high-spending, event-led visitors.
items.source: Campaign Middle East, on the ATM Travel Trends Report 2026 (with Tourism Economics)

figures.label: Middle East-bound travellers prioritising luxury (51% elsewhere)
Event travellers citing cultural events (42% elsewhere)
UAE travellers booking several hotels in one destination

keyPoints: 77% of people interested in visiting the Middle East prioritise luxury when booking, against 51% of those considering other destinations.
Among event-led visitors, 55% cite cultural events and 22% religious events, against 42% and 13% for other destinations.
Gulf travellers are curious abroad too: about two-thirds of UAE and Saudi travellers try to learn some of the local language, the highest of 14 markets in Hilton's research.
81% of UAE travellers book more than one hotel within a single destination.
body: The Arabian Travel Market Travel Trends Report 2026, produced with Tourism Economics, an Oxford Economics company, profiles who is coming to the region and why. Its core finding is that the Middle East attracts a distinctly premium, experience-led visitor, with luxury and cultural events weighing far more than for other destinations. The article does not give the sample size.

Campaign Middle East's coverage also draws on Skift and Hilton research: 42% of MENA travellers are classed as cultural-immersion travellers, and UAE travellers often split stays between neighbourhoods (52%) or mix budget and luxury hotels (46%).
items.relevance: Tourism boards, airlines, hotels and luxury brands in the Gulf are courting high-value, event-driven visitors. Airport, landmark and city-centre OOH around major events is where that audience can be met in person.

pitch.line: 77% of travellers interested in the Middle East prioritise luxury when booking, against 51% of those heading elsewhere (ATM Travel Trends Report 2026).

study.by: Arabian Travel Market with Tourism Economics

items.headline: Singles Day sales grow just 3.7% to CNY1.68trn as livestreams and AI take the spotlight
items.dek: Syntun's tally across China's main platforms shows a mature festival, with tech leading categories and beauty and luxury resale outgrowing the market.
items.source: WWD, on Syntun's Singles Day 2026 data

figures.label: Total Singles Day sales, all major platforms

keyPoints: Singles Day 2026 sales reached about CNY1.679trn (around $251.7bn) across Tmall, JD.com, Pinduoduo, Douyin and Kuaishou, up 3.7% year on year, according to Syntun.
Technology products took about 30% of sales, apparel 13.8% and personal care and beauty 8.2%; beauty sales on Tmall rose more than 20%, led by Proya and SkinCeuticals.
Luxury resale grew faster than the market: Zhuanzhuan's watches and accessories rose nearly 40%.
AI was the showpiece: 100,000 subscriptions to Alibaba's QwenWork sold in 30 minutes on Austin Li's livestream, and Muji ran 24-hour streams hosted by AI 'digital humans'.
body: With the major platforms no longer publishing detailed totals, third-party tracker Syntun put this year's festival at about CNY1.679trn across the five main platforms, a 3.7% rise. The modest growth confirms Singles Day as a mature, value-driven event rather than the explosive showcase of the last decade.

Within the total, the winners were brands that turned the festival into content. Womenswear label Unica took CNY42m from a six-hour livestream; Vgrass's sales rose more than tenfold after a mime-theatre stream; and in sportswear, Fila, Adidas and Lululemon led Tmall's first-week ranking, with Nike sixth. According to WPIC, AI chatbots drove about 5% of purchases through embedded links in October.
items.relevance: China's biggest sales event is now a low-growth, content-led contest in which livestreams and AI hosts decide who wins share. Brands need fame built before the festival, including in high-footfall city media, to be the ones shoppers and their AI assistants go looking for.

pitch.line: China's Singles Day sales grew just 3.7% in 2026, to about CNY1.68trn across the main platforms (Syntun, via WWD).

items.headline: Australians set to spend a record A$7.2bn over Black Friday weekend, with one in four asking AI for deals
items.dek: A 7,654-person survey for the Australian Retail Council and Roy Morgan shows fewer shoppers spending more each, as early Christmas buying and bargain-hunting rise.
items.source: Roy Morgan and Australian Retail Council, Black Friday–Cyber Monday spending forecast 2026

figures.label: Plan to use an AI chatbot for research

keyPoints: Australians are forecast to spend a record A$7.2bn over the four-day Black Friday weekend, up 5.5% or A$374m on last year.
About 5.8m people plan to shop, slightly fewer than last year's 6m, but the average planned spend has risen 14.4% to A$920 and almost a third plan to spend A$1,000 or more.
Motivations have sharpened: low prices (58%, from 42%), great deals (51%, from 38%) and saving on Christmas gifts (39%, from 25%).
One in four will use an AI chatbot to research products and deals, and 72% of them will be doing so for the first time.
body: The Australian Retail Council and Roy Morgan surveyed 7,654 Australians aged 18 and over by SMS between 15 and 19 October 2026; 1,838 of them planned to shop the sales. The resulting forecast is the largest yet for the 27–30 November event.

Clothing, footwear and accessories (33%), technology (30%) and household goods (29%) top shopping lists. Men plan to spend more on average (A$1,028) than women (A$822), with technology leading men's lists and fashion women's. Two-thirds plan to buy both gifts and items for themselves, and a quarter intend to start Christmas shopping early, up from 14%.
items.relevance: Black Friday has become Australia's main Christmas kick-off, with fewer but bigger-spending shoppers who plan ahead. Retailers that build awareness in the fortnight before the sales, on roadside and retail-precinct OOH as well as in search and AI answers, are best placed to capture that larger basket.

pitch.line: Australians plan to spend a record A$7.2bn over the 2026 Black Friday weekend, up 5.5%, with average planned spend up 14.4% to A$920 (Australian Retail Council and Roy Morgan).
