items.headline: Global agrees to buy Alight Media, adding 1,500 digital 48-sheets to its UK real-world media estate
items.dek: Global is expanding into roadside digital and leisure venues by acquiring the challenger founded in 2019 by former Clear Channel Europe chief Matthew Dearden.
items.source: Global, company release
keyPoints: Global has agreed to buy Alight Media, whose estate includes more than 1,500 digital 48-sheets, digital and classic 6-sheets and over 4,000 screens in leisure and hospitality venues.
The deal is subject to regulatory approval and is expected to complete in the first quarter of 2027; the two firms operate separately until then.
Alight was founded in 2019 by Matthew Dearden, a former president of Clear Channel Europe, and Dave Huckerby.
Alight's inventory will be plugged into Global's DAX and Global IQ systems and its AdPower self-serve platform.
The price was not disclosed.
body: Global, which entered OOH in 2018 by buying Primesight, Outdoor Plus and Exterion and holds the rail advertising contract for Transport for London, has agreed to acquire Alight Media. Alight has built one of the UK's fastest-growing digital estates since 2019: more than 1,500 digital 48-sheets, a network of digital and classic 6-sheets and more than 4,000 digital screens in leisure and hospitality settings.

Global says the businesses will stay independent until completion, expected in the first quarter of 2027 subject to regulatory approval. Simon Pitts, Global's group chief executive, said the company was 'delighted' to agree the deal; Alight's co-founder Matthew Dearden called it the next phase of growth. The combined offer will be sold through Global's data, programmatic and self-serve tools. The price was not disclosed.
items.relevance: Consolidation is reshaping the UK's real-world media market: Global adds roadside digital scale and venue audiences to its transport and city-centre portfolio. Buyers should expect fuller national digital packages from fewer sellers, and competitors to respond with pricing and data.

pitch.line: Global's acquisition of Alight Media adds more than 1,500 digital 48-sheets and 4,000 venue screens to its UK OOH estate (Global).

links.label: The Media Leader: Global to acquire Alight Media

items.headline: Inglewood voters narrowly reject a SoFi-backed bid to scrap 60 digital billboards
items.dek: A ballot measure that would have overturned the city's 20-year deal with WOW Media is failing by under 900 votes, keeping one of Los Angeles's biggest digital roadside programmes alive for now.
items.source: Billboard Insider
keyPoints: A ballot initiative backed by SoFi Development to ban advertising on public property in Inglewood is failing, with 52% voting no.
Passage would have overturned the city's 20-year agreement with WOW Media for 60 digital billboards.
Only 889 votes separate the sides and certification is not expected until late November.
Courts have upheld the WOW Media deal, but SoFi Development has appealed.
Mayor James Butts, who backs the deal, appears headed for a March run-off against Gloria Gray.
body: The long-running fight over Inglewood's digital billboards, pitting the city and its media partner WOW Media against SoFi Development, owner of the stadium district, went to voters last week. The SoFi-backed initiative would have barred the city from allowing advertising on public property, unwinding its 20-year agreement for 60 digital billboards.

With 52% voting no, the measure is on course to fail, but the margin is only 889 votes and the result will not be certified until late November. Courts have so far upheld WOW Media's contract, though SoFi has appealed. Ronald Camhi of Michelman & Robinson told Billboard Insider a defeat would be 'a meaningful development' for WOW and the wider industry.
items.relevance: Municipal advertising rights remain politically contested in the US. Media owners bidding for city programmes need local political and community support, not just the best financial offer.

pitch.line: Inglewood's 20-year deal for 60 WOW Media digital billboards survived a ballot challenge with 52% voting no (Billboard Insider).

items.headline: SAMDecaux and Shanghai Hongqiao open a 141 m² micro-LED 'Gilded Theatre' for cultural content
items.dek: The airport and JCDecaux's Shanghai joint venture have installed a glasses-free 3D digital stage in Terminal 2, reserved for non-commercial, public-interest storytelling.
items.source: The Moodie Davitt Report
keyPoints: Shanghai Hongqiao and SAMDecaux have unveiled a 141 m² micro-LED installation, the 'Gilded Theatre', in Terminal 2's Central Tunnel.
It combines an entrance screen and a concourse screen using micro LED-in-package technology with more than 99% display consistency.
Content is exclusively non-commercial and public-interest, including glasses-free 3D art and an immersive sound system.
The launch piece, 'Up! Shanghai', mixes Shikumen architecture, plane trees and the skyline, echoing the CIIE theme of openness.
The airport handles close to 50 million passengers a year.
body: Shanghai Hongqiao International Airport and SAMDecaux, JCDecaux's joint venture with Shanghai Airport Authority, have opened a digital stage in the Central Tunnel of Terminal 2. The 141 m² installation pairs an entrance screen with a concourse screen built on micro LED-in-package technology, and adds day-and-night visual sequences and an immersive sound system.

The screens carry only non-commercial, public-interest content. The opening work, 'Up! Shanghai', features Shikumen houses, plane trees, magpies and an aircraft symbolising international links, with a night version showing lanterns and dancing on the Huangpu. The project is framed within China's 'Four Characteristics Airport' policy for safe, green, smart and humane development.
items.relevance: Chinese airports are using premium digital canvases to build place-branding as well as revenue. Cultural programming of this kind raises the perceived quality of the environment, which helps the commercial screens around it command premium prices.

pitch.line: Shanghai Hongqiao and SAMDecaux have installed a 141 m² micro-LED stage in Terminal 2, at an airport handling close to 50m passengers (Moodie Davitt).

items.headline: Santa Monica approves an eighth Promenade digital screen, a 30-year deal for Orange Barrel Media
items.dek: The council has backed a curved 1,000 sq ft display on the vacant Junipher Building, with the city taking at least $500,000 a year or 20% of advertising revenue.
items.source: Santa Monica Daily Press
keyPoints: Santa Monica's council has approved the eighth digital display in its Third Street Promenade district, on the vacant 1912 Junipher Building.
The applicant, XYZ Now, is represented by Orange Barrel Media; the curved screen measures about 1,000 sq ft (roughly 55ft by 18ft).
The city receives a $500,000 community benefit up front, then the greater of 20% of gross advertising revenue or $500,000 a year, rising 3% annually.
The term is 30 years with two 10-year renewal options, and about 20% of screen time is reserved for city and art content.
The district allows up to 16 screens, projected to earn the city $3.5m–7m a year if all are built.
body: Santa Monica's city council has approved a curved digital display of about 1,000 sq ft on the landmark Junipher Building at 1355 Third Street Promenade, the eighth screen under the Downtown Digital Display District ordinance passed in January. The applicant, XYZ Now, is represented by Orange Barrel Media.

The terms illustrate how US cities are monetising downtown digital: a one-off $500,000 community benefit, then the greater of 20% of gross advertising revenue or a $500,000 annual minimum rising 3% a year, plus $30,000 for Promenade improvements. The deal runs for 30 years with two 10-year options, and about a fifth of airtime goes to civic and art content. The district allows up to 16 screens.
items.relevance: Revenue-sharing, civic airtime and long terms are becoming the template for US downtown digital districts. Media owners that can pair landmark sites with credible place-making will win these programmes.

pitch.line: Santa Monica will take the greater of 20% of gross ad revenue or $500,000 a year from its eighth Promenade digital display (Santa Monica Daily Press).

items.headline: US OOH industry donates space for a national 'Hate Has No Home Here' campaign
items.dek: The OAAA has teamed up with Robert Kraft's Blue Square Alliance Against Hate, asking members to donate billboards, digital screens and transit sites to a nationwide public-service campaign.
items.source: Billboard Insider, on an OAAA release
keyPoints: The OAAA and the Blue Square Alliance Against Hate have launched a national public-service campaign under the line 'Hate Has No Home Here'.
OAAA members are asked to donate billboards, digital screens and transit inventory across all markets.
Creative is available in traditional and digital formats via the OAAA's public-service portal.
The initiative was led by Drew Katz, chief executive of Interstate Outdoor Advertising and an OAAA board member.
body: The OAAA has partnered with the Blue Square Alliance Against Hate, founded by Robert Kraft in 2019, on a nationwide public-service campaign carrying the message 'Hate Has No Home Here'. Members are being asked to donate static billboards, digital screens and transit inventory, with creative supplied for both traditional and digital formats.

The effort was spearheaded by Drew Katz of Interstate Outdoor Advertising. Anna Bager, the OAAA's chief executive, and Robert Kraft fronted the launch. Neither the number of sites nor the value of donated media has been disclosed.
items.relevance: Donated public-service campaigns reinforce the medium's civic role and goodwill with city authorities, which matters when contracts and permits are up for renewal.

items.headline: Courtside Media Network turns UAE padel courts into an advertising network
items.dek: A Dubai start-up is selling branding on court glass, fences and nets, with a pipeline of nearly 200 courts in a country that has about 30% of Asia's padel courts.
items.source: Campaign Middle East
keyPoints: Courtside Media Network has launched in Dubai, selling advertising on padel court glass, fences and nets.
It has a pipeline of nearly 200 Dubai courts, sold in Standard, Gold and Premium tiers; these are pending partnerships rather than live inventory.
The UAE has about 1,000 padel courts, roughly 30% of Asia's total.
The company was founded by Karim Mohamed, Amir Borro and Jad Chamoun.
body: Padel's rapid growth in the Gulf has produced a new real-world media format. Courtside Media Network, a Dubai start-up, is packaging branding on court glass, fencing and nets into a network sold in three tiers. It says it has close to 200 courts in its Dubai pipeline, although these are partnerships still being signed rather than live inventory.

The UAE has around 1,000 padel courts, about 30% of Asia's total, and the sport draws a young, affluent, socially active audience. The founders, Karim Mohamed, Amir Borro and Jad Chamoun, are positioning the network as premium lifestyle media.
items.relevance: Sport venues are becoming addressable real-world media networks. For brands targeting affluent Gulf residents, padel offers dwell time and community, though buyers should check live inventory and audience verification before committing.

pitch.line: The UAE has about 1,000 padel courts, roughly 30% of Asia's total, now being packaged as an ad network (Campaign Middle East).

brief: Consumers are feeling the squeeze: only 38% of adults across 33 countries feel financially comfortable, says Ipsos, yet Accenture finds holiday shoppers ready to let an AI agent spend about $100 without asking.

Marketers are counting the cost of AI as well: Forrester expects a third of AI projects to be shelved next year, and a WU Vienna and Frankfurt School study finds ChatGPT ads earn webshops a third of what Google search delivers.

In real-world media, office lobby screens draw 3.4 times the attention of other small-format DOOH, Korea's OOH market reaches a record ₩4.65trn, Spanish OOH outgrows television, and New Tradition, Frame OOH and Australia's Bishopp all go shopping for sites.

Diary: Ströer reports on 12 November, SPT's Glasgow bus shelter tender closes and FIRB's oOh!media deadline falls on 13 November, Fraport Bulgaria's lounge EOI closes on 15 November, oOh!media's takeover goes to court on 18 November, and Schiphol's €426m advertising tender closes on 20 November.

numberOfDay.line: Office lobby screens earn 3.4 times the attention of comparable small-format DOOH in roadside, retail and transport settings (Lumen Research for ECN).

steal.title: Sell what happens after the ride
steal.text: Oricom's survey of 1,000 Japanese rail users finds 60% of those who recall a train ad go on to research or consider the product, and B2B ads drew the strongest response. The idea worth stealing: pitch transit campaigns on the action they prompt, not just the eyeballs, pairing station and carriage posters with a search or QR follow-up and reporting the lift in branded searches during the run.

items.headline: Only 38% of consumers worldwide feel financially comfortable, Ipsos finds
items.dek: Ipsos's Cost of Living Monitor, covering 33 countries, shows two-thirds expect inflation to stay abnormal beyond next year. Britain records the sharpest fall in financial comfort.
items.source: Ipsos, Cost of Living Monitor 2026

figures.label: Expect inflation to stay abnormal past next year
Expect higher energy bills within six months

keyPoints: Across 33 countries, only 38% of adults say they are financially comfortable or doing alright; 32% are just getting by and 27% find it difficult.
Two-thirds (65%) think inflation will not return to normal until after next year, or never, and 68% expect it to rise over the coming year.
Great Britain shows the steepest drop in financial comfort since last year, down eight points.
76% blame wars and conflicts for driving inflation, and 70% expect to pay more for energy within six months.
Lower-income households are hardest hit: 38% find it difficult, against 24% who are comfortable.
body: Ipsos interviewed 23,531 adults online in 33 countries between late August and early September for its annual Cost of Living Monitor. The global average paints a picture of lasting strain: 38% are comfortable or doing alright, 32% are just getting by and 27% are struggling. The gap by income is stark, with 38% of lower-income households finding it difficult.

Consumers do not expect relief soon. Some 65% believe inflation will not return to normal until after next year, or never, and 68% expect it to rise in the coming year. Majorities also expect higher unemployment (57%), taxes (57%) and interest rates (53%), while 70% anticipate bigger energy bills in the next six months. Three-quarters see war and conflict as the main driver of rising prices.

Country detail matters. Great Britain has the biggest fall in those feeling comfortable, down eight points; 41% of French adults expect their standard of living to fall; and 35% of Americans expect their disposable income to shrink. Ipsos notes the global figure is an unweighted average of countries.
items.relevance: With most consumers squeezed, value messaging and reassurance close to the point of purchase gain weight. Brands that keep investing in visibility while rivals cut tend to gain share as confidence recovers.

pitch.line: Only 38% of adults across 33 countries feel financially comfortable (Ipsos Cost of Living Monitor 2026).

chart.title: What consumers expect over the next year

items.headline: Holiday shoppers are ready to let AI agents spend $100 without asking
items.dek: Accenture's survey of more than 16,000 shoppers in ten countries finds four in ten will use generative AI for holiday shopping. Yet half still plan to split their spending evenly between shops and online.
items.source: Accenture, Holiday Shopping 2026

figures.label: Will use gen AI for holiday shopping
Average an agent may spend unapproved
Category spend likely influenced by gen AI
Plan to split spend evenly, stores and online

keyPoints: Four in ten holiday shoppers will use generative AI this season, up from three in ten last year, according to Accenture's survey of 16,000+ shoppers in ten countries.
Shoppers would let a personal AI agent spend an average of $102 without approval; active gen AI users would allow $149.
Three in ten trust a personal AI agent more than themselves to shop, rising to one in two among active users.
Physical retail holds firm: half expect to split spending evenly between stores and online, and 44% go to shops to see, touch and try products.
Average planned spend is $737, up 12% year on year, with 53% citing rising costs as the reason.
body: Accenture surveyed more than 16,000 shoppers aged 18 to 80 across ten countries, including 4,048 in the US, between 13 August and 1 September. Its headline: shoppers are increasingly willing to hand the gift list to AI. Four in ten will use generative AI this season, and they expect it to influence around 45% of category spending. Deal-finding (39%), comparing options (31%) and picking the best retailer (30%) are the main uses.

Trust in delegation is growing. Shoppers would let an agent spend $102 on average without approval, and three in ten trust a personal agent more than themselves. Among US shoppers, nearly three-quarters want agents to buy only from brands they prefer or know, which makes existing brand familiarity a gatekeeper in agentic commerce.

The physical store is not being written off. Half of shoppers expect to split holiday spending evenly between stores and online; 44% visit to see and try products, 35% value taking a purchase home immediately and 32% go for inspiration. In the US, 21% say AI has made their store trips more intentional.
items.relevance: If agents shortlist only familiar brands, mental availability built before the search begins matters more. Real-world media near shops also catches the 32% who still visit stores for gift inspiration.

pitch.line: Holiday shoppers would let an AI agent spend $102 on average without asking for approval (Accenture).

chart.title: Why holiday shoppers still visit stores

items.headline: Agency strategists regain influence, but more of them now fear AI will replace them
items.dek: WARC's Future of Strategy 2026, based on 489 agency strategists, finds their sway with clients rising and optimism returning. Yet the share who worry AI will eventually take their jobs has jumped from 41% to 56%.
items.source: WARC, via Marketing Dive

figures.label: Strategists who see clear reasons for optimism
Fear AI will eventually replace them
Say they need stronger evidence of business impact

keyPoints: Half of agency strategists now say strategy has real influence with clients, up from 41% a year ago, according to WARC's survey of 489 strategists.
Two-thirds (66%) see clear reasons for optimism, and 65% say AI frees time for more nuanced strategic work.
Anxiety is rising alongside: 56% fear AI will eventually replace them, against 41% last year.
Eight in ten say they must build stronger evidence of business impact, and 57% want a new value proposition and pay model.
WARC's Lena Roland argues that in an age of AI, humanity becomes a competitive advantage.
body: WARC surveyed 489 agency-side strategists in August for its Future of Strategy 2026 report. The mood is markedly better than a year ago: two-thirds see clear reasons for optimism, and the share who say strategy carries weight with clients has climbed from 41% to 50%. The backdrop is grim, however; Marketing Dive notes that the advertising industry shed 6,900 jobs between August 2025 and August 2026, according to Emarketer.

AI cuts both ways. Some 65% say it gives them time for more nuanced work and 55% expect it to refocus strategy on human perspectives. But 56% now worry that AI will eventually replace them, a sharp rise from 41% last year.

The report's prescription is accountability. Eight in ten strategists say they need stronger proof of business impact, and 57% believe the discipline needs a new value proposition and compensation model. WARC's Lena Roland told Marketing Dive the tide 'may be turning', but stressed that the problems are not yet solved.
items.relevance: Strategists who must prove business impact will favour channels with robust effectiveness evidence. OOH sellers who bring econometric and brand-lift proof, rather than reach alone, will find a more receptive audience in planning teams.

pitch.line: 80% of agency strategists say they must build stronger evidence of business impact (WARC Future of Strategy 2026).

chart.title: How agency strategists feel

bars.label: AI frees time for strategic work

report.label: The Future of Strategy 2026

items.headline: ChatGPT ads earn webshops a third of what Google search delivers
items.dek: A working paper from WU Vienna and Frankfurt School, using data from nearly 1,900 online shops, finds ChatGPT visitors convert at a third of Google's rate. At current prices, the economics do not add up for most advertisers.
items.source: WU Vienna and Frankfurt School of Finance & Management, via Adformatie
keyPoints: Paid ChatGPT visitors generated $0.89 of revenue each, against $2.45 for Google search ads, in data from nearly 1,900 webshops.
ChatGPT visitors converted at 0.37%, versus 1.17% for Google, and spent $74 less per order.
Matching Google's return would require a cost per click of about 26 cents; the actual average is $1.72.
84% of the 100-plus webshops tracked in detail received no orders from ChatGPT ads.
body: Maximilian Kaiser of WU Vienna and Christian Schulze of the Frankfurt School of Finance & Management analysed anonymised data from almost 1,900 international webshops with combined annual revenue of $16bn. Their 73-page working paper, Can Advertising Fund Free AI, compares the rollout of ChatGPT ads in the US and UK with Europe, where ads arrived later, and tracks more than 100 shops in detail.

The results are stark. A paid ChatGPT visitor produced $0.89 of revenue against $2.45 from Google search ads; conversion was 0.37% versus 1.17%, and average orders were $74 smaller. To match Google, ChatGPT clicks would need to cost about 26 cents, but the average is $1.72 and OpenAI advises bids of $3–5. Of the shops tracked closely, 84% saw no ChatGPT ad orders, and one large advertiser accounted for 70% of recorded purchases.

The authors also question the wider business model: OpenAI's projection of about $102bn in ad revenue by 2030 implies some $40 per free user a year, against roughly $1 today and serving costs of about $5. OpenAI had not responded, and Adformatie notes that smaller Dutch tests reported better results.
items.relevance: Early evidence suggests conversational AI ads are not yet a dependable performance channel, so marketers should treat them as tests rather than shift proven budgets. It is a reminder to judge new ad formats on outcomes, not novelty.

pitch.line: A paid ChatGPT visitor brings webshops $0.89 in revenue, against $2.45 from Google search ads (WU Vienna / Frankfurt School).

study.by: Maximilian Kaiser (WU Vienna) and Christian Schulze (Frankfurt School of Finance & Management)

chart.title: Revenue per paid visitor

items.headline: Forrester: marketers will scrap a third of their AI projects as the bills arrive
items.dek: Forrester's 2027 predictions say usage-based pricing will force B2C leaders to cut back AI initiatives. Most US marketing chiefs also expect their AI to cause a brand-damaging incident within a year.
items.source: Forrester, Predictions 2027

figures.label: AI initiatives expected to be scaled back
US B2C marketers expecting an AI brand incident
Say leaders demand more proof of AI value

keyPoints: Forrester predicts B2C marketing leaders will scale back about a third of their AI initiatives in 2027 as usage-based vendor pricing makes every prompt and agent action a billable event.
64% of US B2C marketing executives believe their AI use will probably cause a brand-damaging incident within 12 months.
78% say leadership now demands more evidence of AI's value than a year ago, and 82% expect to justify future AI spending more rigorously.
Half of brands will make human-generated content a top priority again to rebuild trust.
About one in 20 US and UK consumers will shift routine buying to conversational, agent-led purchasing.
body: Forrester's 2027 predictions for B2C marketing, CX and digital describe an AI reality check. As martech vendors move to usage-based pricing, each generated asset, agent interaction and automated workflow carries a cost, and Forrester expects marketers to cut about a third of their AI initiatives, with finance and procurement taking a bigger say.

Its Q3 2026 CMO Pulse Survey of US B2C marketing executives underpins the call: 82% expect to give stronger justification for AI investment, 78% say leadership wants more evidence than a year ago, and 64% think their AI use will likely cause a brand-damaging incident within the next year. Forrester also expects AI agents to replace legacy marketing and insight tools at one company in ten.

On the consumer side, Forrester forecasts that half of brands will put human-generated content back at the top of their priorities to build trust amid a flood of AI output, and that roughly one in 20 US and UK consumers will move routine purchases to conversational, agent-led shopping.
items.relevance: As AI budgets face scrutiny, channels with transparent costs and proven brand effects become easier to defend. Human-made, physically present creative in real-world media fits the trust agenda Forrester describes.

pitch.line: 64% of US B2C marketing chiefs expect their AI use to cause a brand-damaging incident within a year (Forrester).

chart.title: US B2C marketing executives on AI

links.label: Forrester blog: CMOs reckon with an AI reality check

items.headline: One social post in four is now an ad, and repeated creative can cut conversions by 60%
items.dek: WPP Media's New Rules of Social Creative, drawing on new research with Snap and Ipsos, warns that half of consumers find fully AI-made brand content soulless.
items.source: WPP Media, with Snap and Ipsos research

figures.label: Share of social posts that are ads
Find fully AI-made brand content soulless

keyPoints: One in four posts a consumer sees on social media is now an ad, up from one in fifteen in 2015, according to WPP Media.
Repeated exposure to identical creative can cut conversion rates by as much as 60%.
Research by WPP with Snap and Ipsos finds 50% of consumers find fully AI-generated brand content soulless and 70% find hyper-personalised ads intrusive.
A System1 study cited by WPP found the top 20% of creators drove 45% of brand memory uplift.
body: WPP Media's briefing on the new rules of social creative draws on a client learning session and new consumer research commissioned with Snapchat and Ipsos. Its starting point is clutter: one post in four in a social feed is now an ad, against one in fifteen a decade ago, and showing the same creative repeatedly can cut conversion by up to 60%.

The research also sets limits on automation and targeting. Half of consumers say fully AI-generated brand content feels soulless, and 70% find hyper-personalised ads intrusive. WPP cites a GOAT Agency campaign in which a 90% increase in creative assets, through a wider variety of creators, coincided with a 255% rise in return on ad spend.
WPP Media does not publish the sample size or markets of the Snap and Ipsos research, so the consumer figures should be treated as indicative.
items.relevance: Crowded, hyper-targeted feeds strengthen the case for uncluttered, shared real-world media. The finding that consumers dislike intrusive personalisation also supports contextual rather than individual targeting in DOOH.

pitch.line: One post in four on social feeds is now an ad, up from one in fifteen in 2015 (WPP Media).

items.headline: Office lobby screens earn 3.4 times the attention of other small-format DOOH
items.dek: A Lumen Research study for ECN finds screens in office buildings beat roadside, retail and transport placements on attention and lift brand recall by 44%. The gap has widened since the previous wave.
items.source: Executive Channel Network and Lumen Research, via Outsmart
keyPoints: ECN's D6 office screens earned 3.4 times the attention of comparable D6 screens in roadside, retail and transport settings, up from 2.5 times in the previous study.
The advantage was 8.3 times against transport screens and 5.9 times against shopping malls.
Even against large-format digital roadside such as 48- and 96-sheets, office screens earned 1.25 times the attention on average.
Office screens generated 44% more brand recall than standard D6 DOOH.
Lumen attributes the result to repeated exposure through the working week.
body: Lumen Research tested 603 full-time office workers in the UK, France and Germany and compared the results with its database of more than 100 OOH and digital studies, at 95% confidence. The headline is that the same 2m² screen earns far more attention in an office lobby or lift area than on the street, in a mall or in a station.

The gains have grown since the earlier wave: the multiple against transport rose from 6.2 to 8.3 and against malls from 4.4 to 5.9. Lumen's Mike Follett notes that the screens sit where office workers walk and wait every day, allowing attention to accumulate. The study was published by ECN, which sells the screens.
items.relevance: Attention varies sharply by environment, not just by format, so planners should buy OOH by context. Office-based DOOH offers a hard-to-reach, affluent B2B and professional audience with high dwell time.

pitch.line: Office lobby screens earn 3.4 times the attention of comparable small-format DOOH elsewhere and 44% more brand recall (Lumen Research for ECN).

chart.title: Attention earned by ECN office D6 screens vs other environments

items.headline: Four in five disabled Britons rarely see themselves in OOH advertising
items.dek: Research by JCDecaux Reach and The Diversity Standards Collective finds disabled people see OOH more often than others, yet feel even less represented in it than in media overall. Nine in ten would favour brands that include them.
items.source: JCDecaux Reach and The Diversity Standards Collective, via Outsmart

figures.label: Disabled people rarely or never represented in OOH
More likely to consider an inclusive brand
Physically disabled people seeing OOH 4+ times a week

keyPoints: 80% of disabled people rarely or never see themselves represented in OOH advertising, compared with 72% across all media.
91% of disabled people would be more likely to consider a brand that featured a disabled person or story in an OOH campaign; so would 74% of non-disabled respondents.
Disabled audiences are heavier OOH viewers: 43% of people with physical disabilities and 41% of neurodiverse people see it at least four times a week, against 28% of non-disabled people.
One in three disabled people say they pay moderate or higher attention to OOH ads.
The disabled Purple Pound is put at £274bn a year, or up to £446bn including household spending.
body: The study, titled Representation in the Real World, sets out what its authors call a disability gap in advertising. The gap is wider for OOH than for media as a whole, which is striking because disabled audiences are among the medium's most frequent viewers.

The commercial case is laid out plainly: inclusion lifts brand consideration among disabled and non-disabled people alike. Respondents responded best to portrayals based on lived experience, where disability is part of everyday life rather than the whole story. The release does not give the sample size or fieldwork method.
Rich Miles of The Diversity Standards Collective warns that putting someone in an ad is not the same as genuinely including them.
items.relevance: Representation is a creative brief that OOH sellers can bring to clients with numbers attached: a heavy-viewing audience that feels overlooked, and a consideration lift that extends well beyond it.

pitch.line: 91% of disabled Britons would be more likely to consider a brand that features disabled people in its OOH ads (JCDecaux Reach / Diversity Standards Collective).

study.by: JCDecaux Reach and The Diversity Standards Collective

chart.title: See OOH advertising at least four times a week

items.headline: UK cinema takings jump 35% in October and pass £1bn for the year
items.dek: Box office in the UK and Ireland reached £100.6m in October, and the year to date is running 22% ahead of 2025. A strong slate is drawing crowds into one of the few truly captive real-world media environments.
items.source: The Media Leader, on Rentrak and Digital Cinema Media data
keyPoints: UK and Ireland box office reached £100.6m in October, 35% more than a year earlier, and the year-to-date total passed £1bn to reach £1.07bn.
Year-to-date takings are 22% ahead of 2025 and 31% ahead of 2024.
DCM estimates October admissions rose about 30%, putting the year's admissions roughly 16.5% ahead.
Spider-Man: Brand New Day became 2026's first £100m film.
DCM says its Q1–Q3 revenue is 10% ahead of 2025.
body: Rentrak figures reported by The Media Leader show a broad-based October: only one film, Verity (£11.8m), passed £10m, but eight of the top ten took more than £4m. Tom Linay, head of film at cinema ad sales house DCM, described it as a consistent slate, and estimates admissions rose around 30% year on year; official admissions data follows later in the month.

For the year so far, Spider-Man: Brand New Day leads with £100.3m, ahead of The Odyssey (£88.3m) and Toy Story 5 (£58.5m). DCM, which sells advertising in most UK cinemas, says its revenue for the first three quarters is 10% up on 2025.
The November line-up includes several major releases, and DCM expects at least one more title to pass £10m in the UK.
items.relevance: Cinema is having its best run in years, and audiences in a darkened auditorium are about as attentive as media gets. For real-world media planners, a rising cinema audience is a useful companion to OOH in the Christmas period, around high streets and leisure destinations.

pitch.line: UK cinema takings rose 35% in October and passed £1bn for the year, 22% ahead of 2025 (Rentrak, via The Media Leader).

chart.title: Top UK and Ireland films, October 2026

items.headline: Americans will spend on Christmas, but 42% are more stressed about affording it
items.dek: EY-Parthenon's consumer sentiment survey finds gift budgets holding up even as shoppers cut back on eating out and wait for deals. It forecasts the strongest holiday sales growth since 2021.
items.source: EY-Parthenon, via PR Newswire

figures.label: Plan to spend same or more on gifts

keyPoints: EY-Parthenon forecasts US November–December retail sales up 5.2% to $1.08trn, the strongest growth since 2021.
62% plan to spend the same or more on gifts than last year, yet 42% feel more stressed about affording them.
Nearly half are cutting back on restaurants and entertainment, and about a third on electronics and travel.
41% plan to buy themselves a present, rising to 53% among 19–34s.
14% expect to carry holiday debt into 2027.
body: The seventh wave of EY-Parthenon's bimonthly US Consumer Sentiment Survey, covering more than 1,500 consumers, paints a picture of determined but stretched shoppers. Most plan to buy for as many people as last year (81% the same number or more), and physical gifts (51%) are favoured over experiences (21%).

The trade-offs fall elsewhere: almost half are reining in spending on restaurants and entertainment. If prices rise, 27% say waiting for promotions will be their main strategy, and around a quarter are already holding out for deals. EY's retail lead, Mark Chambers, says shoppers are starting earlier to spread the cost.
Self-gifting is a notable sub-theme, especially among younger adults, and 14% expect to carry holiday debt into the new year, most of them hoping to clear it by spring.
items.relevance: A deal-hungry, early-starting shopper rewards brands that are visible near stores and on the commute throughout the season, not just on Black Friday. Price and promotion messaging in real-world media close to the point of sale fits this mood.

pitch.line: 62% of Americans will spend the same or more on gifts this year, but 42% are more stressed about affording them (EY-Parthenon).

chart.title: US holiday intentions, 2026

items.headline: Nearly half of Americans have yet to start their holiday shopping
items.dek: Coresight Research's weekly tracker finds 48.5% of US consumers had not begun buying gifts, up on the same point last year, though the gap is narrowing. Walmart is widening its lead over Amazon.
items.source: Coresight Research
keyPoints: 48.5% of US consumers had not started their holiday shopping by early November, against 44.5% at the same point in 2025.
Coresight says progress is moving closer to last year's pace.
Walmart is widening its lead over Amazon as a holiday destination, according to the tracker.
The survey tracks retailers shopped and categories bought each week, compared with the same weeks of 2025.
body: Coresight Research surveys roughly 400 US consumers every week through the season, asking whether they have started holiday shopping, what they bought in the past seven days, where and in which categories. The latest wave shows a later start than in 2025: 48.5% had yet to begin, four points more than a year earlier, though the gap is closing.
The tracker also points to Walmart pulling further ahead of Amazon. Detailed category and retailer figures sit behind Coresight's paywall and are not reported here.
items.relevance: With half the market still to start, the bulk of holiday persuasion is still ahead. Late-season campaigns near stores and in high-footfall areas can still reach shoppers who have not yet decided where to buy.

pitch.line: Almost half of US consumers (48.5%) had not started holiday shopping by early November, up from 44.5% a year ago (Coresight Research).

items.headline: 31.2 million Americans watched midterm election night, the most since 2018
items.dek: Nielsen's Big Data + Panel estimate puts primetime coverage across 13 networks well above 2022, though short of 2018's peak. Over-55s made up almost two-thirds of the audience.
items.source: Nielsen
keyPoints: An estimated 31.2 million people watched primetime midterm coverage on 3 November 2026, up from 25.4 million in 2022 but below 36.1 million in 2018.
The audience peaked at 32.4 million in the 9:30pm ET half hour.
Broadcast networks took 57% of viewing and cable 43%.
Adults 55+ accounted for 19.7 million viewers, against 7.5 million aged 35–54 and 2.9 million aged 18–34.
21.6 million households tuned in, a 16.9 rating.
body: Thirteen networks carried election coverage from about 8pm to 11pm Eastern time, and Nielsen's estimate, using the Big Data + Panel measurement it introduced in September 2025, puts the combined audience at 31.2 million. That is a clear rise on 2022 and 2014 but below 2018 and 2010.

The age profile is stark: over-55s supplied almost two-thirds of viewers, while 18–34s numbered fewer than three million. Several networks simulcast on streaming services such as ABC News Live, Paramount+, Peacock and Fox One, but the release does not split out streaming viewing.
The figures close a campaign in which political advertising set records, much of it on TV and connected TV.
items.relevance: Live news events still gather mass, but older, TV audiences. Younger voters and consumers have to be reached elsewhere, including in the street and on their phones, which is a useful point for OOH sellers pitching reach among under-35s.

pitch.line: 31.2 million Americans watched midterm election-night coverage, but only 2.9 million of them were aged 18–34 (Nielsen).

chart.title: US midterm election-night TV audience

items.headline: Spanish adspend rises 4.1% to €4.4bn, and OOH outgrows television
items.dek: InfoAdex data for January to September show outdoor up 5.3% while TV barely moves and linear TV falls 4.3%. Social and search lead the digital surge.
items.source: InfoAdex, via IPMARK
keyPoints: Spain's measured media investment reached €4,406.9m in January–September 2026, up 4.1%, according to InfoAdex.
OOH grew 5.3% to €346.6m, well ahead of television (+0.3%).
Linear TV fell 4.3% to €1,014m; social media rose 12.4% and search 9.5%.
Digital formats now account for €2,537.6m, against €1,869.3m for non-digital.
Cinema was the fastest-growing medium at +15.1%, albeit from a small base.
body: InfoAdex's figures for the first nine months of 2026 show Spanish media investment of €4,406.9m, up 4.1% on €4,234.9m a year earlier. Television remains the largest medium at €1,225.7m but grew only 0.3%; strip out connected formats and linear TV fell 4.3% to €1,014m.

Digital drove most of the gain. Search rose 9.5% to €717.1m and social media 12.4% to €643.6m, while websites added 6.4%. Digital formats together reached €2,537.6m, comfortably ahead of non-digital at €1,869.3m.
Among traditional media, OOH stood out, rising 5.3% to €346.6m. Radio and digital audio grew 1.4%, while newspapers (−2.0%) and magazines (−3.4%) declined. Cinema rose 15.1% to €15.1m.
items.relevance: Spain joins the list of markets where OOH is growing faster than television, a useful data point in budget conversations. Sellers can position real-world media as the traditional channel still gaining share while linear TV contracts.

pitch.line: Spanish OOH investment rose 5.3% in January–September while television grew just 0.3% (InfoAdex).

chart.title: Spain media investment growth, Jan–Sep 2026

items.headline: Half of the French object to ads woven into creators' content
items.dek: Kantar Media's latest TGI France survey of 15,000 people finds 52% oppose advertising and product placement by creators, against 22% who don't mind. The same data show a strong preference for meeting in person.
items.source: Kantar Media, via The Media Leader FR
keyPoints: 52% of French people aged 15+ say they oppose advertising and integrated product placement by content creators; only 22% say it does not bother them.
Three-quarters (76%) prefer meeting in person to meeting virtually.
Among music-streaming subscribers, price is the deciding factor for 46%, ahead of catalogue size (37%).
Only 4% belong to a fandom, but 42% of those follow creators and 34% buy merchandise.
12% visited a coffee chain in the past year; 61% of them went to Starbucks.
body: TGI France, run by Kantar Media, surveys a representative sample of 15,000 people aged 15 and over and tracks more than 60,000 variables. Its latest release, reported by The Media Leader FR, carries an uncomfortable message for the creator economy: a majority of the French (52%) say they oppose advertising and product placements built into creators' content, while just 22% are relaxed about it.

The survey also points to an enduring taste for physical presence. Some 76% prefer in-person meetings to virtual ones. Elsewhere, price leads the criteria for music-streaming subscribers (46%), followed by catalogue size (37%), genre range (30%) and audio quality (28%). Fandoms remain niche at 4% of the population, though they are commercially active: 42% of fans follow creators and 34% buy merchandise, with music, film and series, and video games the most unifying worlds.

Smaller findings round out the picture. Some 12% visited a coffee shop chain in the past year, with Starbucks (61%), Columbus Café & Co (32%) and McCafé (22%) the most visited, and 87% of pet owners treat their animal as a family member, though only 8% insure its health.
items.relevance: French audiences are sceptical of paid creator integrations, so brands leaning heavily on influencer spend should balance it with channels that are openly advertising and broadly accepted. A strong preference for in-person contact also supports media that meets people in physical spaces.

pitch.line: 52% of French people oppose ads and product placements inside creators' content; only 22% don't mind (Kantar Media TGI France).

chart.title: French attitudes to creator advertising

items.headline: German Christmas sales to edge up 2%, but gift budgets stall at €262
items.dek: The HDE retail federation forecasts €129.2bn in November–December turnover, with online growing twice as fast. Shoppers plan to spend roughly what they did last year, and non-food retailers are gloomy.
items.source: HDE (Handelsverband Deutschland), via retail-news.de
keyPoints: Germany's retail federation expects November–December sales of €129.2bn, up 2% in nominal terms, with online rising 4.1% to €23.1bn.
The average gift budget is €262 per person, €1 less than last year.
Among 2,000+ consumers, over half will spend the same as in 2025, 10% more and 24% less.
56% of non-food retailers expect a weaker Christmas than last year.
body: Handelsverband Deutschland (HDE) forecasts that German retail turnover in November and December will reach €129.2bn, a nominal rise of 2% that includes price effects. Online is expected to outpace the total, growing 4.1% to €23.1bn.

The consumer side is flat rather than festive. In an HDE survey of more than 2,000 people, the average planned gift budget is €262, against €263 last year. Just over half intend to spend the same as in 2025, 10% plan to spend more and 24% less.

Retailers are more pessimistic. Of 300 companies surveyed, 56% of non-food retailers expect a weaker Christmas than last year. HDE president Alexander von Preen called continued willingness to buy gifts a positive signal, while pointing to heavy burdens from energy, staff costs and bureaucracy.
items.relevance: With gift budgets static, German Christmas will be a battle for share rather than a rising tide, so visibility close to the point of purchase matters. Store-adjacent OOH and retail media can help retailers win the decisive moment as shoppers shift more spend online.

pitch.line: Germans plan to spend €262 each on Christmas gifts, flat on last year, as sales edge up 2% to €129.2bn (HDE).

items.headline: Italian brands spend 10% more on creators as mid-tier fees climb
items.dek: Kolsquare's Budget Report 2027 finds Italian influencer investment up 10.4% this year, driven by volume rather than price. Across Europe, 89% of brands plan bigger creator budgets in 2027.
items.source: Kolsquare, via Engage
keyPoints: Italian investment in influencer collaborations rose 10.4% in 2026, driven by more activity and ambassador deals rather than higher list prices.
Fees for creators with 100,000–500,000 followers rose 9.2%, while mega-creators' Instagram fees fell for a third year.
89% of European brands plan to increase influencer budgets in 2027; median spend rose from €127,000 to €144,000.
Paid social is getting dearer too: ad costs rose 16% on TikTok, 13% on YouTube and 12% on Meta.
body: Kolsquare's Budget Report 2027, reported by Engage, shows Italian brands spent 10.4% more on influencer collaborations in 2026. The report stresses that growth reflects more campaigns and longer ambassador contracts rather than price inflation: average fees per post rose 2.45% on Instagram and 1.23% on YouTube and slipped 0.33% on TikTok.

Pricing is shifting by tier. Fees for mega-creators (over a million followers) fell on Instagram for the third year running, while creators with 100,000 to 500,000 followers raised prices by 9.2%. YouTube long-form video is the most expensive format and Instagram Stories the cheapest; a single long-form video by a mega-creator generates a median earned media value of €73,835.

Across Europe, influencer collaborations average 7.8% of company turnover, median company spend rose from €127,000 to €144,000, and 89% of brands plan to spend more in 2027. Paid social is also inflating, with ad costs up 12% on Meta, 16% on TikTok and 13% on YouTube.
items.relevance: Rising costs across both creator fees and paid social squeeze the efficiency of social-first plans. That strengthens the case for diversifying into broad-reach channels, such as OOH, whose prices are not set by platform auctions.

pitch.line: 89% of European brands plan to raise influencer budgets in 2027, as Italian creator spend grows 10.4% (Kolsquare).

chart.title: Rise in social ad costs

items.headline: Dutch over-60s are moving to Instagram and TikTok as Facebook fades
items.dek: Intelligence Group's quarterly tracker shows Facebook's favourite-platform score falling 15 points in three years, while Instagram gains across every age group. Facebook still leads among the over-50s, but its lead is narrowing.
items.source: Intelligence Group, via Adformatie

figures.label: Facebook as a favourite, all ages

keyPoints: The share of working Dutch people naming Facebook among their favourite platforms fell 14.9 points to 43% between Q3 2023 and Q3 2026.
Instagram overtook Facebook among 30–50-year-olds in early 2024 and now stands at 66.6%, against Facebook's 45.4%.
Instagram rose 9.5 points to 40.3% among the over-60s and 8.5 points to 48.1% among 51–60s.
TikTok jumped from 32% to 48% among the under-30s and gained about five points among over-60s.
The study measures preference, not usage, so a falling score does not automatically mean lost reach.
body: Intelligence Group surveys the Dutch working population every quarter, and the Academie voor Arbeidsmarktcommunicatie compared rolling annual averages to Q3 2023 and Q3 2026. Facebook has slid furthest: its favourite-platform score fell 14.9 points to 43% overall, and among 30–50-year-olds from 61.5% to 45.4%, as Instagram rose from 57.8% to 66.6%.

The shift is reaching older users. Instagram gained 8.5 points among 51–60-year-olds, to 48.1%, and 9.5 points among the over-60s, to 40.3%. TikTok rose 5.1 points among the over-60s and leapt from 32% to 48% among the under-30s, where Instagram already sits around 77%.

Facebook still leads among the over-50s, but its margin is shrinking. Adformatie notes a caveat: the survey records which platforms people favour, not how often they open them, so falling popularity need not mean Facebook is losing users or ad reach.
items.relevance: Assumptions that older audiences live on Facebook are becoming outdated in the Netherlands, so age-based channel rules need refreshing. Marketers targeting the over-50s should test Instagram and keep broad-reach media in the mix as social habits fragment.

pitch.line: Facebook's standing as a favourite platform among Dutch workers fell 15 points in three years, as Instagram won over the over-60s (Intelligence Group).

chart.title: Instagram as a favourite platform, Q3 2026

items.headline: Korea's OOH market hits a record ₩4.65trn, with digital at 38%
items.dek: Official statistics from the Korea Outdoor Advertising Center show the market edged up 0.5% in 2025 while digital OOH grew 6.1%. Elevator advertising was the stand-out, up 28%.
items.source: Korea Outdoor Advertising Center, via Korea Newswire
keyPoints: South Korea's OOH market reached a record 4.6472 trillion won in 2025, up 0.5%, according to the country's only nationally approved OOH statistics.
Digital OOH grew 6.1% to 1.7649 trillion won, lifting its share of the market from 36.0% to 38.0% in a year.
Building-mounted advertising remains the largest format at 1.99 trillion won (42.9% of the total), up 6.0%.
Advertising in public places grew fastest among the main formats (+11.9%), driven by elevator screens and panels, up 28.1% to 161.9bn won.
The industry employs 43,986 people, up 1.6%, of whom 85% work in production and installation.
body: The Korea Outdoor Advertising Center, part of the Korea Local Government Finance Cooperative, published its 2026 OOH statistics (covering calendar 2025) on 30 October; the figures were distributed by Korea Newswire and reported by Asia Economy on 3 November. The series, compiled annually since 2017, combines a sample survey of 2,000 OOH businesses with a census of all 243 local governments.

Headline growth was modest, but the mix is shifting. Digital OOH rose 6.1% to 1.7649 trillion won and now accounts for 38% of the market, two points more than a year earlier. By format, building-mounted signage is still dominant at 1.9916 trillion won, followed by transit facilities (517.9bn won), vehicles (413.7bn won) and printed graphics (391.4bn won). Public-place advertising grew 11.9% to 305.4bn won, with elevator advertising up 28.1%.

Production and installation generated 2.9577 trillion won (+2.3%) and media sales and agency work 1.6895 trillion won. The centre's director, Cha Byung-jun, said the continued growth of digital showed the industry's 'growth potential and capacity for change'.
items.relevance: Korea offers a clear benchmark for how fast digital can grow its share of a mature OOH market even when overall spend is flat. The surge in elevator media points to the value of residential and office proximity formats that reach people in daily routines.

pitch.line: Digital now accounts for 38% of South Korea's record ₩4.65trn OOH market, up from 36% a year earlier (Korea Outdoor Advertising Center).

study.by: Korea Outdoor Advertising Center (Korea Local Government Finance Cooperative)
study.sample: 2,000 OOH businesses; census of 243 local governments

chart.title: Korean OOH revenue by format, 2025

items.headline: Six in ten Japanese commuters act on train ads they remember
items.dek: An Oricom survey of 1,000 rail users in Tokyo and Kansai finds that most people who recall a train ad go on to look it up or consider the product. Young commuters and B2B advertisers see the strongest response.
items.source: Oricom, via MarkeZine

figures.label: Took action after recalling a train ad

keyPoints: 60% of Japanese rail users who spontaneously recalled a train ad then did something about it, such as researching or considering the product, according to agency Oricom.
In greater Tokyo, 15–29-year-olds were the most responsive; 51% of them looked up the ad's content.
Men responded more than women, significantly so in Kansai (68% vs 48%); in Tokyo the gap (63% vs 56%) was not statistically significant.
B2B ads produced an 83% action rate and 59% researched the content, though from a small base of 29 responses.
There was no significant difference between the Tokyo and Kansai regions overall.
body: Oricom, a Japanese agency specialising in transit media, surveyed 1,000 people aged 15 to 69 who live in greater Tokyo or Kansai and ride trains at least weekly, using the Knowns consumer panel between 26 and 30 June 2026. This second release from the study, published on 2 November, looks at what people did after seeing a train ad they could recall unprompted; an earlier release linked recall to the total number of days ads ran and how fresh the placements were.

Overall, 60% took some related action, measured as the share who did not answer 'none of these'. In Tokyo, action rates varied significantly by age and peaked among 15–29s, the majority of whom went on to research the ad. In Kansai there were no significant differences by age, but a marked gender gap: 68% of men acted against 48% of women.
By industry, B2B advertising stood out, with an 83% action rate and 59% researching the content. Oricom flags this as indicative only, as it rests on 29 responses.
items.relevance: The study gives transit sellers evidence that memorable train ads lead to search and consideration, not just awareness, which supports pairing rail OOH with search and social retargeting. The strong B2B result suggests commuter rail deserves a place on business-audience plans.

pitch.line: Six in ten Japanese commuters who recall a train ad go on to research or consider the product (Oricom).

chart.title: Share who acted after recalling a train ad, by gender

items.headline: Small-town India's Gen Z finds brands on Instagram, but buys on family advice
items.dek: MSL India and Youth Ki Awaaz polled 3,509 under-30s in tier 2–4 cities. Social media drives discovery, yet family and friends remain the most trusted voice, and TV and print barely register as a first touchpoint.
items.source: MSL India and Youth Ki Awaaz, via afaqs!

figures.label: Spend under ₹5,000 a month on themselves

keyPoints: 55.8% of young Indians in tier 2–4 cities first hear of products they later buy on Instagram, against just 5.4% via TV or print ads.
Family and close friends are the most trusted source before a purchase (73.1%), well ahead of reviewers (49.1%) and big influencers (28.0%); celebrities trail at 9.5%.
Small creators carry more weight than large ones: 48% consider a small creator they follow, against 35.5% for large creators.
More than 62% use quick-commerce apps at least weekly and 84.5% pay online regularly.
Bad product experiences (59.6%) and greenwashing (35.7%) are the main reasons trust in a brand breaks.
body: 'Bharat Z Vibe Check', the second edition of MSL India's study of young people beyond the metros, surveyed 3,509 respondents under 30 in tier 2, 3 and 4 cities through Youth Ki Awaaz's WhatsApp-based polling platform, Yoot. It was published on 4 November.

Discovery is overwhelmingly digital: Instagram (55.8%) and YouTube (39.0%) lead, followed by e-commerce apps (29.8%) and search (23.2%). But purchase decisions are relational. 73.1% trust family and friends most, and 49.0% say they try new brands because the name has long been familiar. 54.8% trust Reels and short-video ads, though 18.6% say no ad format builds trust, with women more sceptical than men.

Budgets are tight, with 67.7% spending under ₹5,000 a month on themselves, mostly on food delivery and eating out (58%) and travel (44.1%). Around 60% bought, sold or swapped second-hand goods in the past year, and half pay for an OTT service.
items.relevance: For brands chasing India's next wave of consumers, long-term familiarity and word of mouth matter as much as social reach. Highly visible, consistent real-world presence in smaller cities can build the name recognition that half of this audience says drives trial.

pitch.line: 73% of young Indians in tier 2–4 cities trust family and friends most before buying something new (MSL India / Youth Ki Awaaz).

study.by: MSL India and Youth Ki Awaaz

chart.title: Where young small-city Indians first discover products

items.headline: Amazon reaches 9.5 million Australian shoppers as Temu and Shein gain and eBay slips
items.dek: Roy Morgan data for the year to June 2026 show Amazon adding 728,000 shoppers, while Temu and Shein also grew. eBay and Kogan lost customers.
items.source: Roy Morgan, via B&T
keyPoints: Amazon had 9.5 million Australian shoppers in the 12 months to June 2026, up 728,000 and three points in shopper incidence, according to Roy Morgan.
Temu grew by 371,000 shoppers to 5.1 million, and Shein by 433,000 to 3.0 million.
eBay lost 389,000 shoppers to 5.9 million, and Kogan.com fell by 58,000 to 1.2 million.
Amazon and Temu customers each shopped about six times a year, while eBay's shopping frequency declined.
Roy Morgan's chief executive, Michele Levine, said Amazon is 'now part of the establishment'.
body: Roy Morgan's latest retail data, reported by B&T on 6 November, track shopper numbers, incidence and frequency for Australia's largest online marketplaces over the year to June 2026.

Amazon was the clear winner, adding 728,000 shoppers to reach 9.5 million, while also increasing how often customers buy. China-linked platforms continued to grow: Temu added 371,000 shoppers (to 5.1 million) and Shein 433,000 (to 3.0 million), each gaining two points of incidence. The losers were eBay, down 389,000 to 5.9 million, and Kogan.com, down 58,000 to 1.2 million.
Levine described Amazon as 'no longer just a disrupter', noting that it is growing its customer base and the frequency of use at the same time.
items.relevance: As marketplaces consolidate their hold on Australian online spending, brands and local retailers need to compete for consideration before shoppers reach the platform. Roadside and retail OOH remains one of the few ways to build demand outside the marketplaces' own ecosystems.

pitch.line: Amazon now reaches 9.5 million Australian shoppers, up 728,000 in a year, while eBay lost 389,000 (Roy Morgan).

chart.title: Australian shoppers by marketplace, 12 months to June 2026

items.headline: UAE Gen Z keeps going out, even on a budget
items.dek: Research from Platinumlist and Udora finds that seven in ten young people in the UAE spend on in-person meet-ups every week. Cheaper tickets are taking a bigger share of event sales.
items.source: Platinumlist and Udora, via Communicate

figures.label: Budget AED500+ a month for going out
Tickets under AED100, share of sales
Think digital can replace real life

keyPoints: 71% of Gen Z respondents in the UAE spend money on in-person social meet-ups at least once a week, despite budget pressure.
68% set aside at least AED500 a month for going out, events and gifts; dining and concerts are each cited by 60% as favourite ways to reconnect.
More than 90% say their digital lives give them more reasons to meet in person, and only 10% think digital contact can replace real-life interaction.
79% regularly feel the need to put their phones away.
Tickets under AED100 rose from about 55% to 67% of UAE event ticket sales in the first half of 2026, while those above AED500 fell from about 9% to 5%.
body: The ticketing platform Platinumlist and the experience-discovery app Udora surveyed Gen Z respondents in the UAE about how they spend their social time and money; Communicate reported the findings on 8 November. The sample size and method were not disclosed.

The headline finding is that young people treat real-world experiences as a priority rather than a luxury: 71% spend on in-person meet-ups weekly and a further 18% two to three times a month. Most say online life prompts offline plans rather than replacing them, and nearly eight in ten often want to put their phones away.

Platinumlist's ticket data show the trade-off. Lower-priced tickets (under AED100) grew from about 55% to 67% of sales in the first half of 2026, while premium tickets above AED500 fell from about 9% to 5%. Spending on going out is holding up, but it is shifting towards cheaper, more frequent experiences.
items.relevance: Gen Z's appetite for frequent, affordable outings keeps them moving through malls, venues and leisure districts, which favours OOH near entertainment and dining hubs. Brands can borrow the 'phones down' sentiment by building real-world activations rather than relying only on screens.

pitch.line: 71% of UAE Gen Z spend on in-person meet-ups every week, even under budget pressure (Platinumlist and Udora).

chart.title: UAE event ticket sales by price, H1 2026

items.headline: MENA is the world's most optimistic region about AI and jobs
items.dek: The FII Institute's Priority Compass, run with Ipsos across 32 countries, finds two-thirds of people in Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Morocco expect generative AI to create more good jobs than it destroys. Only 27% of Europeans agree.
items.source: FII Institute and Ipsos, via Communicate

figures.label: MENA: AI will create more good jobs

keyPoints: 66% of respondents in MENA believe generative AI will create more quality jobs than it destroys, against 46% globally, 33% in North America and 27% in Europe.
Global optimism is slipping: 46% agree this year, down from 49% last year.
85% of respondents worldwide support a global framework of rules for AI, and 80% reject AI making final decisions in hiring, justice or healthcare.
71% in the Global South would pay for AI classes, against 36% in the Global North.
The MENA findings draw on Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Morocco, where samples skew urban, educated and affluent.
body: The fifth edition of the FII Priority Compass, produced by the Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute with Ipsos, interviewed 61,200 people in 32 countries between 24 April and 5 June 2026. Communicate reported the findings on 3 November.

The regional divide on AI is stark. Two-thirds of MENA respondents expect generative AI to create more quality jobs than it removes; Asia and Africa stand at 57%, North America at 33% and Europe at 27%. In the Global North, 70% disagree. Confidence about personal job security follows the same pattern: 66% in the Global South expect their jobs to survive AI, against 56% in the Global North.

Enthusiasm comes with caveats. 85% want global rules for AI, 80% reject AI taking final decisions in sensitive areas, and 61% believe humans will lose control of advanced AI within 20 years. The report notes that samples in Saudi Arabia and Morocco are not nationally representative and reflect more urban, educated and affluent people.
items.relevance: Optimistic, AI-curious audiences in the Gulf give brands more room to lead with AI-powered products and services than in Europe. Messages should still stress human oversight, which most respondents everywhere want.

pitch.line: 66% of people in MENA expect generative AI to create more good jobs than it destroys, against 27% in Europe (FII Institute / Ipsos).

chart.title: Believe generative AI will create more quality jobs than it destroys

items.headline: Six in ten Brazilians plan to shop on Black Friday, and many are planning with AI
items.dek: Surveys from Opinion Box with Dito, and from Google Brasil, show Brazilian shoppers drawing up lists early and expecting to spend more than last year. Half still plan to shop in physical stores.
items.source: Opinion Box, Dito and Google Brasil, via Propmark

figures.label: Plan to shop on Black Friday
Expect to spend more than in 2025

keyPoints: 62% of Brazilians plan to shop on Black Friday on 27 November, 24% are undecided and 14% will not buy, according to an Opinion Box and Dito survey of 1,000 people.
Google Brasil's annual study finds 41% expect to spend more than in 2025, and 48% already have wish lists before campaigns begin.
70% have not yet chosen a retailer, leaving the field open; only 30% know where they will buy.
Electronics (43%), appliances (39%) and clothing (39%) top intended purchases.
Shoppers plan to use e-commerce sites (63%), apps (59%) and physical stores (50%).
body: Propmark brought together two pre-Black Friday studies on 2 November. Opinion Box and the CRM firm Dito surveyed 1,000 people online in July and August: 62% intend to buy, chiefly electronics, appliances, clothing, travel (34%) and beauty (33%). Google Brasil's annual survey, for which no sample was given, adds detail on how shoppers are preparing.

Planning starts early and increasingly involves digital tools, including AI. 44% have already started checking prices and 48% have lists ready. Half deliberately wait for Black Friday because they trust the date, and 60% see it as the year's best chance to buy higher-value items. 69% expect their finances to improve over the next six months.
Loyalty is up for grabs: 70% have not chosen a retailer. Google Brasil's retail director, Gleidys Salvanha, said success 'will not come from the biggest discount offered'.
items.relevance: With most Brazilian shoppers still undecided about where to buy and half planning store visits, the weeks before Black Friday are a window for retailers to win consideration with high-reach media, including OOH near shopping centres and on commuter routes.

pitch.line: 70% of Brazilian Black Friday shoppers have yet to choose a retailer (Google Brasil, via Propmark).

study.by: Opinion Box with Dito; Google Brasil

chart.title: Where Brazilians plan to research or buy on Black Friday

items.headline: Brazilian cinema advertising audience passes 90 million as attendance holds up
items.dek: Ancine data show 115.9 million cinema admissions in Brazil so far this year, slightly ahead of 2025. Flix Media, which takes over 90% of cinema ad investment, says its audience has grown by more than 15%.
items.source: Ancine and Flix Media, via Propmark
keyPoints: Brazilian cinemas sold 115.89 million tickets between 1 January and 21 October 2026, up from 115.48 million in the same period of 2025, according to Ancine.
Box office reached R$2.46bn, against R$2.3bn a year earlier.
Flix Media, which accounts for more than 90% of cinema ad investment in Brazil, says its audience grew by more than 15% and has already passed 90 million, matching its total for 2025.
The September Semana do Cinema promotion drew 5.6 million viewers, and 'The Devil Wears Prada 2' alone carried 328 ad campaigns.
Flix's network covers 2,269 screens in 143 Brazilian municipalities.
body: Propmark reported on 3 November that the cinema sector is pushing for a bigger share of Brazil's advertising investment, citing official data from Ancine, the national film agency, alongside figures from Flix Media and the organisers of industry promotions.

Attendance is steady rather than spectacular, at 115.89 million admissions to 21 October, but box-office revenue is up to R$2.46bn. Flix Media, the dominant cinema ad seller with over 90% of the medium's investment, says its audience grew by more than 15% year on year. Big releases such as 'The Devil Wears Prada 2' (about 7 million viewers) and four titles including 'Toy Story 5' and 'Michael', which together reached more than 40 million Brazilians, have driven demand.

Flix's chief executive, Cristiano Persona, said the company had recorded 'the biggest monthly revenue in our history'. Promotions such as the Semana do Cinema, which attracted 5.6 million viewers, are being used to bring audiences back to theatres.
items.relevance: Cinema is a real-world, high-attention medium that sits naturally alongside OOH on plans aimed at going-out audiences. Brazil's stable attendance and blockbuster-driven peaks offer predictable moments for brands to combine screens in theatres with nearby mall and street OOH.

pitch.line: Brazilian cinemas sold 115.9 million tickets by 21 October, slightly more than a year earlier (Ancine, via Propmark).

items.headline: China Duty Free's profits rise by a fifth even as sales slip
items.dek: CTG Duty Free's attributable net profit rose 24.6% in the third quarter and 20.3% over nine months, helped by better margins, while revenue fell as Chinese consumer sentiment stayed soft.
items.source: CTG Duty Free (CDFG), via TRBusiness
keyPoints: CDFG's Q3 attributable net profit rose 24.6% to RMB563.6m, and nine-month profit 20.3% to RMB3.67bn, after a double-digit fall in 2025.
Revenue fell 4.7% to RMB11.2bn in Q3 and 2.6% to RMB38.8bn over nine months, reflecting weaker consumer sentiment.
Its share of Hainan's offshore duty-free market rose by more than two percentage points.
International business grew 71%, helped by the acquisition of DFS's Greater China retail business.
body: CTG Duty Free, the operator behind China Duty Free Group, reported unaudited attributable net profit of RMB563.6m (about $84m) for the third quarter of 2026, up 24.6%, and RMB3.67bn for the nine months, up 20.3%. TRBusiness attributes the improvement mainly to margins, following a year in which profit fell by double digits.

Sales remain under pressure. Operating income fell 4.7% to RMB11.2bn in the quarter and 2.6% to RMB38.8bn over nine months, despite strong travel to destinations such as Hainan, where cross-border passenger trips rose 29% in the first half and foreign nationals made up 55.1% of them.

CDFG said its share of the Hainan offshore duty-free market rose by more than two points, and its international business grew 71%, partly reflecting its purchase of DFS's Greater China retail business. It has also opened, with Shanghai Pudong airport, what is described as China's largest airport duty-free zone for domestic brands.
items.relevance: China's travel retail giant is making more money from less revenue, so brands should expect tougher terms and a focus on margin. The rise in foreign visitors to Hainan widens the audience for airport and island advertising beyond Chinese shoppers.

pitch.line: CDFG's Q3 net profit rose 24.6% even as revenue fell 4.7% (TRBusiness).

chart.title: CDFG year-on-year change, 2026

items.headline: Frankfurt Airport courts India-bound travellers with its first Diwali campaign
items.dek: Fraport is running digital, in-terminal and security-area promotions, coupons and personal shoppers in Terminal 1 to capture last-minute gift buying among the 1.2 million passengers a year on its India routes.
items.source: Fraport, via TRBusiness
keyPoints: Frankfurt Airport is marking Diwali with a retail campaign for the first time, aimed at passengers flying to India from Terminal 1.
The campaign combines a digital push with Air India and Lufthansa, terminal touchpoints, security-area promotions, coupons and personal shoppers.
Retail staff receive intercultural training to serve Indian travellers.
More than 1.2 million passengers flew on Frankfurt–India routes in 2025.
body: Fraport has launched Frankfurt Airport's first Diwali campaign, targeting passengers departing for India from Terminal 1 with offers for last-minute gifts for family and friends. The airport says a large share of India-resident passengers buy gifts there.

The activity runs across several touchpoints: an English-language digital campaign with Air India and Lufthansa, selected spaces in the terminal, promotions in the security area, coupons and deals from shops and restaurants on the way to the gate, and personal shoppers. Staff at participating retailers have received intercultural training.
Babett Stapel, Fraport's senior executive vice-president for retail and real estate, said the aim is to translate cultural contexts into a respectful, inspiring experience before departure.
items.relevance: Airports are segmenting by route and culture, not just by terminal. Brands targeting diaspora or festival gifting can align airport media and retail offers to specific flight banks and occasions.

pitch.line: Frankfurt Airport launched its first Diwali campaign for the 1.2 million passengers a year on its India routes (TRBusiness).

items.headline: Harkey Media becomes Frame OOH and plants its flag in Times Square
items.dek: The Phoenix-based roadside operator has relaunched as an independent national OOH platform, buying 9 Times Square in New York and entering Chicago with four digital bulletins on the I-294.
items.source: Frame OOH, via Digital Signage Today
keyPoints: Harkey Media has rebranded as Frame OOH and repositioned itself as an independent national OOH platform operating in 11 US markets.
It has acquired 9 Times Square in New York, relaunched with a new full-motion screen measuring 27ft by 66ft.
It has entered Chicago by buying four 20ft-by-60ft digital bulletins on the Tri-State I-294 tollway, plus two static wallscapes.
The company has also opened a New York office.
Chief executive Scott Harkey says the aim is to own great frames in great markets.
body: Harkey Media, a Phoenix-based billboard company, has relaunched as Frame OOH, presenting itself as an independent national platform rather than a regional roadside operator. It now operates in 11 US markets and has opened an office in New York.

The headline asset is 9 Times Square, which Frame has acquired and relaunched with a new full-motion screen of 27ft by 66ft. At the same time the company has moved into Chicago, buying four large digital bulletins (20ft by 60ft) on the Tri-State I-294 and two static wallscapes.

Chief executive Scott Harkey framed the strategy as owning 'great frames in great markets'; president Matt Molina called the relaunch the next chapter for the company. The move pairs trophy inventory in the US's most-watched media square with high-traffic highway digital, the mix national buyers tend to want.
items.relevance: Independent operators are using trophy sites to win national budgets that usually go to the big three US owners. For buyers, more competition for Times Square and Chicago highway inventory means more options; for sellers, it shows how a rebrand plus a landmark asset can reposition a regional business.

pitch.line: Frame OOH, formerly Harkey Media, now operates in 11 US markets and has bought 9 Times Square (Digital Signage Today).

items.headline: New Tradition buys Connell Outdoor to control the road from Las Vegas airport to the Strip
items.dek: The independent operator has acquired a 40-year-old local billboard business with 88 static and digital faces around Harry Reid International Airport, plus two faces next to LAX.
items.source: New Tradition, via Billboard Insider
keyPoints: New Tradition has acquired Connell Outdoor Advertising, gaining 88 static and digital billboard faces in Las Vegas and two faces beside LAX; the price was not disclosed.
Connell's inventory lines the routes in and out of Harry Reid International Airport and the main roads linking it to the Strip.
New Tradition already runs digital spectaculars on the Strip at BLVD, Elara and The Venetian, and one at Westgate near the convention centre.
Connell vice-president Don Krueger joins New Tradition to expand its Las Vegas business.
The deal adds to a wave of US roadside consolidation this autumn.
body: New Tradition, an independent OOH company founded in 2010 and now active in 16 US markets, has bought Connell Outdoor Advertising, a Las Vegas business owned by Mike Connell for more than four decades. The portfolio comprises 88 static and digital faces, concentrated on the entrance and exit routes of Harry Reid International Airport and the arteries that carry visitors to the Strip, plus two faces adjacent to LAX in Los Angeles. Terms were not disclosed.

The acquisition complements New Tradition's existing digital spectaculars on the Strip, at BLVD, Elara by Hilton Grand Vacations and The Venetian Resort, and at Westgate near the Las Vegas Convention Center. The airport handled nearly 55 million passengers in 2025, and the city drew almost six million convention attendees.

Chief operating officer Bret Richheimer described Las Vegas as a city where brands come to make an impression; Mike Connell said he wanted a buyer that understood the value of the locations. Connell's vice-president, Don Krueger, moves to New Tradition.
items.relevance: Owning the airport-to-Strip corridor alongside Strip spectaculars lets one seller package a visitor's whole journey, an attractive proposition for brands targeting conventions and tourists. It also underlines how independents are consolidating niche, high-value inventory.

pitch.line: New Tradition has bought 88 Las Vegas billboard faces covering the routes from Harry Reid airport to the Strip (Billboard Insider).

items.headline: Bishopp adds 450 sites by buying JAM Outdoor in a bet on regional Australia
items.dek: The roadside specialist's acquisition broadens its network beyond the capital cities, following recent expansion across Victoria and New South Wales and the addition of Avalon Airport.
items.source: Bishopp Outdoor Advertising, via B&T
keyPoints: Bishopp Outdoor Advertising has acquired JAM Outdoor, adding more than 450 advertising sites to its roadside network.
The deal is aimed at brands building regional campaigns or extending national activity beyond the capital cities.
It follows Bishopp's recent expansion across Victoria and New South Wales, including Avalon Airport.
Terms were not disclosed.
body: Bishopp Outdoor Advertising has bought JAM Outdoor, bringing more than 450 sites into its existing roadside network.
