items.headline: B2B buyers pick the winner before they call a salesperson
items.dek: 6sense's survey of 4,611 buyers finds the early favourite wins 82% of the time. Use of AI chatbots in evaluations has actually fallen.
items.source: 6sense, via Business Wire
keyPoints: In B2B, the vendor favoured before any sales contact wins 82% of the time.
92% of eventual winners are on the first shortlist; a vendor left off it has less than a 10% chance.
About 60% of the 10.3-month buying cycle passes before buyers speak to a seller.
81% of buyers used an LLM during evaluation, down from 94% a year earlier; 26% use one to find vendors.
body: 6sense's 2026 Global B2B Buyer Experience Report, based on 4,611 recent buyers in North America, APAC, Continental Europe and the UK and Ireland, underlines how much of B2B purchasing is settled before a salesperson is involved. The favourite at first contact goes on to win 82% of the time, and 73% of buying groups hold vendor preferences before they have even formed.

Buyers' own knowledge (34%) and internal discussions (32%) are the biggest influences before seller contact, followed by LLMs (21%). AI use is maturing rather than exploding: 81% used an LLM somewhere in the process, against 94% last year.
Most buyers keep watching vendors between purchases, typically through their websites, and 56% say justifying the category is as hard as, or harder than, choosing a supplier.
items.relevance: Brand salience decides B2B deals long before the pitch. OOH sellers can use this with B2B clients to argue for always-on, high-visibility presence in business districts, airports and transport hubs where decision-makers form those early preferences.

pitch.line: The B2B vendor favoured before any sales contact wins 82% of the time (6sense Global B2B Buyer Experience Report, 4,611 buyers, November 2026).

items.headline: Energy brands add 6% in value, with State Grid and Shell still on top
items.dek: Brand Finance's Energy 100 is worth $731.2bn. Chinese utilities hold almost half the utilities ranking's value, and Edison and Neste are the fastest risers.
items.source: Brand Finance
keyPoints: The world's 100 most valuable energy brands are worth $731.2bn, up 6% in a year.
State Grid leads at $102.4bn, up 20%, and is also the strongest utilities brand.
Shell is the most valuable oil and gas brand for the 12th year running, at $51.8bn.
Edison is the fastest-growing brand, up 33%; Neste leads oil and gas growth at 17%.
body: Brand Finance's annual Energy 100 shows a sector whose brand value is rising faster than its reputation might suggest. The total climbed from $688.6bn to $731.2bn, with utilities growing slightly faster than oil and gas.

China dominates utilities, holding 44% of the Utilities 50 value. State Grid tops the overall table, while Shell, Aramco, PetroChina and ADNOC lead oil and gas. EDF and Enel represent Europe's utilities near the top.
On brand strength, State Grid scores 92.9 out of 100, ahead of Indonesia's PLN and Malaysia's Tenaga Nasional; Shell leads oil and gas strength, narrowly ahead of PETRONAS and TotalEnergies.
items.relevance: Energy and utility brands are investing in reputation as the transition plays out. They are natural OOH advertisers for corporate and transition messaging, especially in the Gulf, China and South-East Asia, where national champions are strengthening their brands.

pitch.line: The world's 100 most valuable energy brands are worth $731.2bn, up 6% in a year (Brand Finance Energy 100, November 2026).

items.headline: Moutai still rules spirits, while baijiu's second tier stumbles
items.dek: Brand Finance's 2026 drinks rankings put Moutai at $59.6bn and Corona Extra top of beer. Tsingtao is the strongest beer brand and José Cuervo the biggest riser.
items.source: Brand Finance
keyPoints: Moutai remains the world's most valuable spirits brand at $59.6bn, more than twice the value of Wuliangye.
Corona Extra is the most valuable beer brand at $13.9bn; Tsingtao is the strongest, with value up 30% to $4.7bn.
José Cuervo is the fastest riser, up 61% to $1.6bn.
Several baijiu brands fell sharply: Yanghe dropped 46%, Guoyuan 38% and Gujing Gong Jiu 32%.
body: Brand Finance's Alcoholic Drinks 2026 report covers the 50 leading spirits brands, 50 beers and ten Champagne and wine brands. China's baijiu giants still dominate value, with Moutai and Wuliangye far ahead of the field.

Below the top tier, the picture is less comfortable. Several baijiu brands lost a third or more of their value, reflecting weaker domestic premium demand. Tsingtao went the other way, climbing three places to sixth among beers and earning the strongest brand rating in the category.
Elsewhere, Crown Royal is the strongest spirits brand, Moët & Chandon the most valuable Champagne and wine brand at $2.3bn, and Barefoot the strongest wine brand.
items.relevance: Drinks brands are polarising between powerful leaders and weakening challengers. In markets where alcohol advertising is allowed, premium spirits and beer brands remain big buyers of high-impact OOH and airport duty-free media, so this ranking helps target the risers.

pitch.line: Moutai is the world's most valuable spirits brand at $59.6bn (Brand Finance Alcoholic Drinks 2026).

items.headline: One AI-made video ad has the carbon footprint of building a laptop
items.dek: Brandtech Data measured a 30-second generative AI ad at about 120kg of emissions. Video made up 17% of generations but 93% of the footprint.
items.source: The Media Leader, on Brandtech Data research
keyPoints: A single 30-second AI-generated video ad produced about 120kg of emissions, roughly the footprint of manufacturing a laptop.
Video was 17% of the 5,426 generations but 93% of the emissions; images were 74% of generations and 5% of emissions.
Each two-second clip used about 30Wh, around three times a 1,000-word text output.
Electricity alone cost about €4 per clip on a standalone set-up, against a maximum provider price of €0.30.
body: Brandtech Data's study, carried out by Fifty-five and reviewed by Fruggr, tracked the full production of one 30-second ad made with generative AI. It took 5,426 generations, using models including Stable Video Diffusion and CogVideo, and covered inference only, not model training.
The results show how unevenly the footprint falls. Video generation was a minority of tasks but almost all of the emissions, while still images and text were comparatively cheap.

The economics are also striking: the electricity cost of a clip on a standalone set-up was many times the price providers charge, which suggests current video-generation pricing is heavily subsidised.
items.relevance: As AI video production scales, carbon reporting on media and production will matter more to advertisers. Media owners can strengthen their sustainability case by pairing low-energy static or efficient digital OOH with transparent production footprints.

pitch.line: A single 30-second AI-generated video ad produced about 120kg of emissions, roughly the footprint of building a laptop (Brandtech Data, November 2026).

items.source: Omnicom, on RECMA Network Diagnostics 2026
keyPoints: Omnicom Media is ranked No. 1 globally and in all four regions for the second report running, with just under 35% of quali-share.
OMD is the top agency network globally for the 12th consecutive RECMA report.
In Australia, WPP Media leads with 59 points and EssenceMediacom is the only agency with a Dominant profile.
Omnicom Media India is also ranked No. 1 in its market.
body: RECMA's twice-yearly Network Diagnostics rate about 700 agencies in 45 markets on 19 performance indicators. The 2026 edition, announced by Omnicom, places Omnicom Media first globally and in North America, EMEA, APAC and LatAm, with Publicis Media, WPP Media, dentsu and Havas following on quali-share, according to B&T's reporting.

Market tables tell a more varied story. In Australia, B&T reports WPP Media on 59 points, with EssenceMediacom the only Dominant agency and Mindshare leading one-year new business, helped by the $128m Suncorp move. In India, Omnicom Media is ranked first.
Note that the global figures come via Omnicom's own release, so treat its additional claims about billings with caution.
items.relevance: Agency league tables shape who gets pitched and who controls budgets. OOH sellers should map which networks rank as Dominant in each market and prioritise their planning leads in agency outreach.

items.headline: Adding OOH, audio and print lifts brand effects by a third, IPA data shows
items.dek: Bauer Media Outdoor and the IPA analysed 569 campaigns from the Effectiveness Databank. Those using all three channels reported markedly stronger brand and business results.
items.source: Outsmart, on Bauer Media Outdoor UK and IPA research

figures.label: More likely to report big trust gains

keyPoints: Campaigns that combined OOH, audio and publishing reported 33% more brand effects and 8% more business effects than those using none of the three.
They were 69% more likely to report very large gains in brand trust, with perceived quality up 43%.
Emotional creative lifted business effects by 23% when all three channels were used, against 8% for TV.
In fast-growing categories, the three-channel mix delivered 185% more very large brand effects.
body: 'Winning The Great Brand Race', from Bauer Media Outdoor UK and the IPA, draws on 569 campaigns in the IPA Effectiveness Databank between 2010 and 2024. It compares campaigns that used OOH, audio and publishing together with those that used none of them.

The three-channel group reported stronger brand effects across awareness, trust, quality and fame, and were three times as likely to report large activation effects (45% against 15%). Strikingly, the effective campaigns using all three needed a slightly smaller share of budget for brand building (65%, against 73% without them).
The analysis shows association rather than proof of cause, but the pattern is consistent across measures and is strongest in fast-growing categories.
items.relevance: This is a ready-made effectiveness argument for OOH in the mix. Sellers can take it to agencies building brand plans, especially for emotional creative and growth categories, with the IPA's name attached.

pitch.line: Campaigns combining OOH, audio and publishing reported 33% more brand effects than those using none of them (IPA and Bauer Media Outdoor, 569 campaigns, November 2026).

items.headline: British listeners are the least likely to treat video as audio
items.dek: YouGov research for Audion finds UK audiences switch between audio and video formats less than their French, Italian or American peers. Spotify leads in Britain; YouTube elsewhere.
items.source: The Media Leader, on Audion and YouGov research

figures.label: UK: listen to video without watching

keyPoints: 58% of UK listeners switch between audio and video platforms, against 74% in the US.
Only 44% of Britons listen to video without watching it, compared with about two-thirds in France, the US and Italy.
Spotify is the leading digital audio platform in the UK at 52%, while YouTube leads in the US, France and Italy.
Most Spotify listeners also use another platform: 65% in the UK and 76% in the US.
body: The research, carried out by YouGov for the audio ad platform Audion, compares listening habits in four markets. The UK stands out for keeping audio and video more separate.

In the US, France and Italy, about two-thirds of people listen to video content without watching, a sign that YouTube has become an audio platform in its own right. In the UK, Spotify remains the default.
Multi-platform listening is the norm everywhere, which complicates planning for brands that buy audio by platform rather than by audience.
items.relevance: Audio and screens are blurring, which makes reach planning harder. OOH sellers can present the street and commute as a complement to fragmented audio, reaching the same on-the-move audiences at the same moments.

pitch.line: 58% of UK listeners switch between audio and video platforms, against 74% in the US (Audion and YouGov, November 2026).

items.headline: Three in four Britons say the marketing they receive is not for them
items.dek: Optimizely's survey of 1,000 UK consumers finds most feel bombarded with irrelevant, repetitive messages. Marketers admit to launching campaigns before the data is ready.
items.source: Dagens Innovation, on Optimizely research

figures.label: Marketers who launch without enough data

keyPoints: 75% of UK consumers regularly receive marketing that is irrelevant to them.
69% get the same message several times from one company, and 61% say they receive too much marketing.
35% unsubscribe after irrelevant messages, and 42% lose interest in the brand.
Among 100 UK marketers surveyed, 60% launch campaigns before they have enough data.
body: Optimizely's 'The Marketer's Survival Guide' surveyed 1,000 UK consumers and 100 UK marketers. The consumer verdict is blunt: messaging feels too general, too frequent and too repetitive.

The marketer responses help explain why. Most admit to launching campaigns with insufficient data and to moving on without analysing results, while two-thirds say an excess of tools creates extra work.
The marketer sample is small, so those figures are indicative; the consumer findings are the stronger signal.
items.relevance: Personalised channels are suffering from overuse. That supports a case for well-placed, contextual broadcast messages, such as OOH near the point of purchase, which reach people without filling their inboxes.

pitch.line: 75% of UK consumers regularly receive marketing that is irrelevant to them (Optimizely, 1,000 UK consumers, November 2026).

items.headline: One shopper in five has abandoned a retailer over data privacy
items.dek: Usercentrics' State of Digital Trust survey of 11,000 consumers finds deep unease about AI personalisation. Half would pay a premium to brands that are open about their use of data.
items.source: Usercentrics, via Business Wire

figures.label: US consumers who dropped a retailer
UK consumers who dropped a retailer
Would pay a premium for transparency

keyPoints: 21% of US and 19% of UK consumers have stopped using a retail brand because of data-privacy concerns.
71% say AI-driven personalisation feels intrusive, rising to 75% in the US.
52% would pay an average 7% premium to brands that are transparent about how AI uses their data.
60% are uncomfortable with their data being used to train AI.
body: The study, conducted by Sapio Research in March 2026 among 11,000 consumers in the US, UK, Germany, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands and Sweden, was released ahead of Black Friday.

It shows privacy has become a purchasing factor. Only about a fifth rank retail among the top three sectors they trust with personal data, and 74% would stop using a service if their data were misused.
Younger consumers are most willing to pay for transparency: 67% of 18 to 29-year-olds, against 23% of those aged 60 and over.
items.relevance: Privacy fatigue strengthens the case for media that needs no personal data. OOH sellers can pitch privacy-safe reach to retailers worried about tracking and AI personalisation backlash.

items.headline: US shoppers will ask AI for gift ideas but won't let it pay
items.dek: Talkdesk's holiday survey finds three-quarters of Americans plan to use AI assistants, yet only one in ten would let an agent buy without checking. Retailers are racing ahead regardless.
items.source: Talkdesk, via GlobeNewswire

figures.label: Would let AI pay without review

keyPoints: 74% of US holiday shoppers plan to use AI assistants, but only 10% would let an AI agent complete a purchase without reviewing it.
49% would buy from an unfamiliar brand on an AI recommendation.
89% of retail leaders are preparing for agentic shopping, and 58% have already suffered AI errors.
77% of shoppers want AI use disclosed, and 74% want stronger rules.
body: Talkdesk's 2026 AI Holiday Shopping Survey, fielded by Centiment in September, questioned 1,048 US online shoppers and 312 retail directors and above.

The gap between retailer ambition and shopper comfort is wide. Nearly all retailers are deploying AI agents in customer service and preparing for agentic commerce, yet only 15% of shoppers would let an agent pay even with a review step.
Errors are already costing business: 29% of retailers that experienced AI mistakes lost a customer as a result, and 37% do not fully disclose their AI use.
items.relevance: Half of shoppers will try an unfamiliar brand if an AI suggests it, so brand familiarity is now contestable. Established brands need visible, trusted presence, such as OOH in retail districts, to stay on the list.

items.headline: The French use AI more than ever, but trust it less than most
items.dek: VML's tenth Future Shopper study finds AI use in France jumped to 70% this year. Only 27% trust what conversational AI tells them, against 38% worldwide.
items.source: The Media Leader France, on VML Future Shopper 2026
keyPoints: 70% of French consumers used AI this year, up from 54%, yet only 27% trust what conversational AI tells them.
Globally, trust in conversational AI stands at 38%.
48% of French spending is now online, slightly below the 51% global figure.
Only 30% of French consumers would sell their data for a monthly income, against 40% globally.
body: VML's Future Shopper, now in its tenth edition, surveyed 28,000 consumers in 17 countries, 2,000 of them in France, through Censuswide in May and June 2026.
France is adopting AI quickly, led by ChatGPT at 45% usage and by Gen Z, 89% of whom use it. But scepticism runs deeper than elsewhere, and the French are more protective of their data.
The smartphone's share of online purchases fell seven points to 41%, and Facebook remains the preferred social network at 34%, well ahead of TikTok at 13%.
items.relevance: French consumers use AI but do not trust it, which leaves room for trusted, visible brand presence. OOH sellers in France can pair this with the country's privacy-minded attitudes to argue for non-intrusive, data-light reach.

pitch.line: Only 27% of French consumers trust what conversational AI tells them, against 38% globally (VML Future Shopper 2026).

items.headline: German advertisers rank creators first for growth, and DOOH is on the rise
items.dek: The OWM's annual Trendbarometer finds creator advertising has overtaken CTV as the top growth channel. DOOH and search are gaining, while linear TV and print lose ground.
items.source: invidis, on the OWM Trendbarometer
keyPoints: Germany's leading advertisers now rank creator advertising as their top growth driver, ahead of CTV and social.
DOOH and search are gaining relevance, while linear TV and print are losing it.
43% of OWM members expect revenue to rise in 2027 and 34% expect higher earnings.
Proving effectiveness across channels remains advertisers' biggest challenge.
body: The OWM, which represents Germany's major advertisers, presented its Trendbarometer at its annual summit. The economic outlook has improved slightly, but budgets are polarising, with fewer members expecting them to stay flat.
Among channels, creator advertising leads, followed by CTV and social. Online video is slipping, retail media and podcasts are stable, and DOOH is among the channels gaining relevance.
Cross-media measurement remains the sector's sorest point. invidis also notes the separate BVDW Trendmonitor, which forecasts DOOH growth of 11%.
items.relevance: German advertisers are moving DOOH up their list, but they want proof. Sellers should lead with cross-media effectiveness evidence and measurement partnerships when pitching German brand owners for 2027.

pitch.line: DOOH is gaining relevance among German advertisers, with the BVDW forecasting 11% growth (OWM Trendbarometer, via invidis, November 2026).

items.headline: Germans are making their peace with ads on free streaming
items.dek: WPP Media and Samsung Ads find acceptance of ads in free streaming has risen to 59%, from 46% in 2023. Paying subscribers are far less forgiving.
items.source: Adzine, on WPP Media and Samsung Ads research

figures.label: Annoyed by ads in paid streaming

keyPoints: 59% of German smart-TV users now explicitly accept advertising in free streaming, up from 46% in 2023.
61% are annoyed by ads in services they pay for.
92% tolerate one spot per break on free services, but only 45% do so on paid ones.
69% would choose a cheaper ad-supported subscription, according to a separate GIK survey.
body: 'Signale vom Sofa', from WPP Media and Samsung Ads, surveyed 3,000 German smart-TV users aged 18 to 69 in May 2026. The headline is growing acceptance: 85% do not reject ads in free streaming.
Tolerance drops quickly with ad load, and much faster on paid services. Three spots per break are acceptable to 43% on free streaming, but to only 11% on paid platforms.
A GIK survey of 1,000 people adds that 56% find ads at the edge of the screen less disruptive than interruptions.
items.relevance: Ad tolerance depends on the value exchange. That is a useful framing for OOH, which funds free public infrastructure and does not interrupt content, and a reminder to keep DOOH loops short.

pitch.line: 59% of German smart-TV users now accept ads in free streaming, up from 46% in 2023 (WPP Media and Samsung Ads, November 2026).

items.headline: Italians save almost half their tech shopping for Black Friday week
items.dek: Teads' Christmas Survey finds 48% of Italian electronics buying falls in the Black Friday period. Shops remain a key discovery channel, especially for the over-55s.
items.source: Youmark, on the Teads Christmas Survey 2026

figures.label: Electronics bought in Black Friday period

keyPoints: Nearly half of Italians' electronics purchases (48.1%) fall in the Black Friday period, up from 46% last year.
Physical stores are a discovery channel for 41.7% of Italians, and for 50.5% of those over 55.
Social media is the leading discovery channel for 47.4% of 18 to 24-year-olds.
Print's role as a source of inspiration fell 2.3 points to 8.8%.
body: Teads surveyed a nationally representative sample of 1,000 Italians in July 2026 and compared the results with a matching 2025 wave.
Black Friday's grip on high-ticket categories is tightening: electronics (48.1%), video games (43.3%) and toys (35.7%) lead, with gift cards also rising.
Review sites and online news are the main inspiration sources, while the shop floor remains powerful for older shoppers.
items.relevance: Italian shoppers concentrate big-ticket buying into one week and still discover products in store. That argues for heavyweight OOH near retail parks and shopping districts in the run-up to Black Friday.

items.headline: A fifth of programmatic ads land on sites 'not suitable for advertising'
items.dek: An audit of campaigns for 22 advertisers in the Netherlands, Belgium and France finds the problem is far bigger than made-for-advertising sites.
items.source: Adformatie, on fma Digital and Spektre research
keyPoints: 20% of programmatic impressions ran on sites deemed 'not suitable for advertising', even though they pass standard brand-safety checks.
Made-for-advertising sites accounted for only 3.4% of impressions.
The unsuitable-site problem is nearly six times as large as the MFA problem.
The audit covered dozens of campaigns for 22 advertisers in the Netherlands, Belgium and France.
body: The media audit agency fma Digital and the inspection platform Spektre examined where programmatic budgets actually end up. Their category of 'Not Suitable for Advertising' covers regular publishers whose content or ad experience makes them a poor environment for brands.
The industry's focus on made-for-advertising sites has missed the larger leak, the authors argue: brand-safety tools filter the obvious offenders but not the low-quality mainstream inventory.
The study is based on audited campaigns rather than a market-wide sample, but it gives advertisers a concrete benchmark.
items.relevance: Waste in open programmatic is a strong argument for verified, premium environments. OOH sellers in the Benelux and France can use it to position audited, brand-safe screens as a home for budgets leaving low-quality web inventory.

pitch.line: One programmatic impression in five lands on sites not suitable for advertising (fma Digital and Spektre, 22 advertisers in the Netherlands, Belgium and France, November 2026).

items.headline: Australian social ad spend grows three times faster than digital
items.dek: We Are Social and Meltwater's Digital 2027 Australia report forecasts US$6.15bn of social ad spend this year. Australians are among the world's most valuable social users to advertisers.
items.source: Campaign Brief, on We Are Social and Meltwater's Digital 2027 Australia
keyPoints: Social ad spend in Australia is forecast to rise 16.5% to US$6.15bn in 2026, three times the 5.5% growth of digital overall.
Advertisers spend US$272 a year per Australian social user, against a global average of US$58, ranking third in the world.
Almost three in ten Australians use ad blockers, and only one in ten feel represented in online ads.
More than seven in ten used generative AI in the past month, but only 8% discovered brands through it.
body: The annual Digital report from We Are Social and Meltwater finds social now accounts for more than 36% of Australian digital ad spend, with 22.6 million social media user identities, almost 83% of the population.
Australians spend nearly 17 hours a week on social platforms, more than twice their 7 hours of linear TV. Instagram and TikTok each take about an hour and three-quarters a day per user.
Streaming is near-universal, with 78.8% watching weekly and 45.5% paying for a service, well above the global rate of 32.4%.
items.relevance: Social is absorbing Australian budgets but faces ad blocking and representation gaps. OOH sellers can position the street as unblockable, shared reach that complements social, with the same audiences on the move.

pitch.line: Advertisers spend US$272 a year per Australian social user, against a US$58 global average (We Are Social and Meltwater, Digital 2027 Australia).

items.headline: Dentsu puts a number on stadium signage: awareness up 12.5% with TV
items.dek: Using AI logo detection and viewer-level TV data, Dentsu found baseball signage lifted brand awareness and favourability, and more so when paired with TV spots.
items.source: Dentsu
keyPoints: Viewers exposed to stadium signage showed 8.5% higher brand awareness than unexposed viewers, rising to 12.5% when they also saw a TV ad.
Favourability rose to an index of 107.5 for signage alone and 110.5 combined with TV.
The tool combines GumGum's Relo Metrics logo detection with Dentsu's STADIA360 TV viewing data.
Formats included backstop signage, helmet logos and interview boards.
body: Dentsu validated its new measurement method on eight Central League baseball broadcasts between late March and late April 2026, with the energy company JERA as title partner. A web survey followed, and viewers were matched at ID level into four groups: signage only, TV ad only, both, and neither.
Against an index of 100 for viewers who saw neither, signage exposure lifted awareness to 108.5 and favourability to 107.5. Combined exposure lifted them to 112.5 and 110.5.
No sample size is disclosed, but the method addresses a long-standing gap: putting brand-effect numbers on in-venue signage seen on broadcast.
items.relevance: Sports signage can now be measured like media. OOH and venue sellers should offer brand-lift evidence with sponsorship packages, and show the extra effect when signage is bought alongside TV.

pitch.line: Stadium signage plus TV lifted brand awareness 12.5% above unexposed viewers (Dentsu, Japanese baseball broadcasts, November 2026).

items.headline: Indian shoppers are among the world's keenest to let AI do the buying
items.dek: McKinsey's agentic-commerce survey of 21,000 consumers in 11 markets puts India second only to China for AI-assisted shopping, led by millennials.
items.source: ANI, on McKinsey's Agentic Commerce Consumer Survey

figures.label: Indian AI users who trust AI tools

keyPoints: 76% of Indian consumers use AI for shopping, second only to China at 80% and far above the 53% global average.
Millennials lead in India at 84%, ahead of Gen Z and Gen X at 74%.
87% of Indian AI users trust AI chat and search tools, against 73% globally.
The survey covered about 21,000 consumers in 11 markets in June 2026.
body: McKinsey's survey shows that India's digital shoppers are moving quickly towards AI-assisted purchasing. Unlike in the West, where Gen Z often leads, millennials are the heaviest users in India.
Trust is the striking difference: Indian users are far more confident in AI tools than the global average, and even global Gen Z (67%) trails them.
The Indian boomer figure (56%) rests on fewer than 100 respondents, so treat it as indicative.
items.relevance: In India, AI may become the first stop for product research faster than elsewhere. Brands need strong offline salience, such as OOH in metros and transit, so that AI shortlists reflect brands consumers already know.

pitch.line: 76% of Indian consumers use AI for shopping, against a 53% global average (McKinsey, 21,000 consumers in 11 markets, November 2026).

items.headline: Quick commerce steals Diwali as festive order volumes rise 21%
items.dek: Unicommerce's analysis of 138 million order items finds quick commerce volumes up 75%. Smaller cities now generate the largest share of orders.
items.source: MediaNews4U, on Unicommerce's festive report
keyPoints: Diwali e-commerce volumes rose 21% year on year, and quick-commerce volumes jumped 75%.
Tier-3 cities accounted for 41% of orders, more than metros and Tier-1 cities combined (34%).
85% of festive orders were worth less than ₹1,000.
Prepaid payments covered 61% of orders, with Tier-3 prepaid volumes up more than 40%.
body: Unicommerce analysed more than 138 million order items processed through its Uniware platform between 6 October and 4 November 2026 and compared them with the same period last year.
Quick commerce was the standout channel, with GMV up 38%. Brands' own D2C sites grew volumes by 30%, while marketplaces grew just 8%.
Growth was fastest in the smallest cities: Tier-3 volumes rose 26%, against 13% in metros and Tier-1 cities.
items.relevance: India's festive demand is shifting to quick commerce and smaller cities. OOH sellers can steer brands towards Tier-2 and Tier-3 town networks and to dark-store catchments where fast delivery now drives impulse purchases.

pitch.line: Quick-commerce order volumes rose 75% during India's 2026 festive season (Unicommerce, 138 million order items).

items.headline: Dubai Mall tops YouGov's UAE ranking, and makes the Saudi top ten too
items.dek: YouGov's BrandIndex mall rankings put Dubai Mall first in the UAE and Al Salam Mall first in Saudi Arabia, narrowly ahead of Jeddah's Red Sea Mall.
items.source: Communicate, on YouGov BrandIndex
keyPoints: Dubai Mall leads UAE mall consideration at 34.4%, ahead of Mall of the Emirates at 29.8%.
In Saudi Arabia, Al Salam Mall leads at 21.9%, a whisker ahead of Red Sea Mall (21.7%) and Mall of Arabia (21.0%).
Dubai Mall ranks seventh in Saudi Arabia, a sign of its regional pull.
Saudi rankings are far tighter than the UAE's, with the top five within two points.
body: YouGov's rankings use nationally representative samples between October 2025 and September 2026 and measure consideration: whether a respondent would consider visiting next time. Only malls tracked for at least a year are included.
In the UAE, Dubai Mall and Mall of the Emirates are well clear of the field, with Dubai Festival City third. Dubai Mall also leads on buzz.
Saudi Arabia's market is more fragmented, with Jeddah and Riyadh malls trading places at the top. Al Salam leads on both consideration and buzz.
items.relevance: Mall media is a key OOH format in the Gulf. These rankings help sellers prioritise malls by consumer pull and show advertisers that Dubai's flagship centres also reach Saudi visitors.

pitch.line: Dubai Mall leads UAE mall consideration at 34.4%, and also ranks seventh in Saudi Arabia (YouGov BrandIndex, November 2026).

items.headline: Gulf brands may have English names, but they advertise in Arabic
items.dek: Data from the AI ad platform Adly shows 92% of ads from Gulf businesses with English brand names are written in Arabic, and luxury language is common.
items.source: Communicate, on Adly data

figures.label: Luxury brand voice: Gulf vs North Africa

keyPoints: 43% of Gulf businesses have English-letter brand names, yet 92% of their ads are in Arabic.
94% of UAE ads created on the platform are in Arabic.
A luxury-oriented brand voice is used by 17% of Gulf businesses, against 5% in North Africa.
Fewer than one Gulf business in 200 mentions free delivery.
body: Adly analysed ads created on its platform between February and October 2026 by businesses in the GCC, the Levant and North Africa. The company notes that its data reflects its own users rather than a random sample.
The finding challenges a common assumption that English branding signals English-first communication. In practice, Arabic dominates ad copy across the Gulf, including in the cosmopolitan UAE.

Regional differences in tone are marked: luxury language is far more common in the Gulf than in the Levant or North Africa, and about nine in ten Gulf advertisers that use numbers prefer Western digits.
items.relevance: International brands entering the Gulf should localise copy into Arabic even when the brand name stays English. That applies to OOH creative as much as digital, where Arabic-first messaging matches local norms.

pitch.line: 92% of ads from Gulf businesses with English brand names are written in Arabic (Adly, November 2026).

items.headline: Brazilians use AI in the middle of the purchase journey, not at the start
items.dek: Troiano and Nico.ag find 85% of Brazilian AI users turn to it at some point when buying, most often after seeing options and when comparing them.
items.source: Meio & Mensagem, on Troiano and Nico.ag research

figures.label: AI users who use it when buying
Use AI after seeing some options

keyPoints: 85% of Brazilian AI users use it at some point in a purchase, most often after they have already seen some options (34.3%).
28% use AI to compare products and 25% for research, rising to 32% when short of time.
Only 11.4% use AI to validate a choice, and 9% after purchase.
The study identifies four AI-user types, led by the 'IApédia' information-seeker (38%).
body: 'As Faces da IA no Brasil' combines 1,200 online interviews with Brazilians aged 18 to 55 across all regions with qualitative ZMET and MOBE sessions.
It finds that AI is a mid-funnel tool: consumers first discover options elsewhere, then bring AI in to narrow and compare them. Almost half rely on it when faced with many choices.
The four personas are IApédia (38%), the do-everything 'Faz-Tudo' (31%), the 'Concierge' (20%) and the 'BFF', who treats AI as a companion (11%).
items.relevance: If Brazilians discover brands before they ask AI, then early awareness decides which brands enter the comparison. That is a strong argument for OOH as a discovery medium in Brazil's big cities.

pitch.line: 85% of Brazilian AI users turn to it at some point in a purchase, mostly after already seeing options (Troiano and Nico.ag, 1,200 interviews, November 2026).

items.headline: Fewer Brazilians plan to shop on Black Friday, and they want deeper discounts
items.dek: Globo's research shows intent to buy fell from 47% to 36% between June and October. Shoppers are researching earlier and will buy before November for the right offer.
items.source: E-Commerce Brasil, on Globo research

figures.label: Intend to buy on Black Friday

keyPoints: Intent to buy on Black Friday in Brazil fell from 47% in June to 36% in October.
65% now expect better discounts than last year, up from 53%.
84% will buy only if prices are truly lower.
32% would buy before November for a good offer, and only 25% are waiting for the day itself.
body: Globo surveyed 2,000 Brazilians between 6 and 9 October and compared the results with a June wave. The mood has cooled and grown more sceptical.
Shoppers are starting earlier: 38% research products three months ahead, up ten points. Interest is rising in electronics, apparel, appliances and self-care.
A separate Nexus survey published the same day found 40% intend to buy, with intent much higher among younger and more educated Brazilians.
items.relevance: Brazilian Black Friday is becoming a season, not a day. Advertisers should start OOH bursts in October and early November, when sceptical shoppers are researching and comparing offers.

pitch.line: Only 36% of Brazilians intend to buy on Black Friday, down from 47% in June (Globo, 2,000 respondents, November 2026).

items.headline: At Aena's airports, food and drink is now outgrowing duty free
items.dek: Aena's third-quarter figures show F&B revenue up 10.2% against 5.9% for duty free. Average spend fell, but a new round of catering tenders points to higher guarantees.
items.source: TRBusiness
keyPoints: F&B revenue at Aena's Spanish airports rose 10.2% in the third quarter, almost twice the 5.9% growth of duty free.
Nine-month retail revenue reached €784m, up 5.8%.
Barcelona (+14.2%) and Madrid (+12.5%) led duty-free growth over nine months, even as average spend fell.
Aena awarded 23 of 28 F&B tenders published this year, and expects minimum guarantees to rise 11% in 2027 and 32% in 2028.
body: Aena's results show the balance of airport commercial income shifting towards catering. Specialty shops grew just 1.4% in the quarter, and average spend per passenger fell, with traffic growth doing much of the work.
Aena's own results put nine-month commercial revenue at €1,574.1m, up 7.4%; TRBusiness reports a different scope. Commercial revenue per passenger rose 4.8% to €5.97.

The catering re-tendering programme is the longer-term story: higher minimum annual guarantees lock in income growth for 2027 and 2028. Aena's advertising concession, meanwhile, still needs re-tendering after its national contract drew no bids in July.
items.relevance: Airport commercial teams are chasing growth through F&B and higher guarantees. Media owners bidding for Aena's advertising should expect the same demand for strong guaranteed returns, and can propose joint F&B and media activations.

pitch.line: F&B revenue at Aena's airports grew 10.2% in Q3 2026, almost twice duty free's 5.9% (TRBusiness).

items.headline: Fraport Bulgaria seeks operators for four lounges at Varna and Burgas
items.dek: Expressions of interest for business and VIP lounges at the two Black Sea airports close on 15 November, for a five-year term with a three-year option.
items.source: Moodie Davitt Report

figures.label: Largest lounge
figures.value: Burgas T1 VIP, 290 sq m + 515 sq m terrace

keyPoints: Fraport Bulgaria is inviting experienced operators to express interest in four airport lounges at Varna and Burgas.
The lounges range from 86 sq m at Burgas T2 to 306 sq m at Varna T1, plus a 515 sq m terrace at Burgas T1.
The concession runs for five years, with an optional three more.
Shortlisted operators will be invited to bid after expressions of interest close on 15 November.
body: Fraport Bulgaria runs the country's two main Black Sea gateways, which handle heavy seasonal leisure traffic. The four lounges are a business or VIP lounge in Varna T2 departures (225 sq m), a VIP lounge in Varna T1 (306 sq m), a business lounge in Burgas T2 (86 sq m) and a VIP lounge in Burgas T1 (290 sq m with terrace).
Expressions of interest are due by 15 November inclusive, after which selected operators will be asked to submit bids.
The tender is a reminder that premium passenger spaces are being commercialised separately at mid-sized European airports.
items.relevance: Lounges are premium environments with valuable audiences. Media owners and brands can approach the eventual operators about sponsored lounge experiences and premium digital screens.

pitch.line: Fraport Bulgaria is tendering four lounges at Varna and Burgas airports, with expressions of interest due on 15 November 2026 (Moodie Davitt Report).

items.headline: Outfront's transit revenue jumps 20% as the World Cup lifts the third quarter
items.dek: The US OOH company grew revenue 9.3% to $511.1m. Its chief executive now expects double-digit revenue growth for 2026.
items.source: Outfront Media, via PR Newswire
keyPoints: Outfront's third-quarter revenue rose 9.3% to $511.1m, helped by FIFA World Cup spending and higher yields.
Transit revenue climbed 20.4% to $135.3m, and transit adjusted OIBDA rose 84.1%.
Billboard revenue grew 5.9% to $373.7m.
Chief executive Nick Brien expects 2026 to be a double-digit revenue growth year.
body: Outfront Media's results confirm a strong year for US OOH. Both segments benefited from the World Cup, held in North America this summer, and from better pricing.
Transit, which includes the New York subway and commuter rail, was the standout, with profits rising much faster than revenue as the business gained scale.
Net income rose 26.3% to $64.8m, and the company declared a quarterly dividend of $0.33 per share.
items.relevance: US OOH is converting big events into growth, and transit is leading. Sellers elsewhere can cite Outfront's transit results when pitching transport networks to advertisers chasing commuters and event audiences.

pitch.line: Outfront's US transit revenue rose 20.4% in Q3 2026, helped by the World Cup (Outfront Media Q3 results).

items.headline: oOh!media shareholders back I Squared's takeover with 99.9% support
items.dek: Australia's largest listed OOH company is set to leave the ASX. A court hearing on 18 November is the last major hurdle before the scheme takes effect.
items.source: Kalkine Media, on the oOh!media ASX announcement
keyPoints: oOh!media shareholders approved I Squared Capital's takeover, with 99.89% of votes cast in favour.
Investors will receive A$1.68 cash per share, less a planned A$0.10 permitted dividend.
The NSW Supreme Court hearing is set for 18 November, with the scheme expected to take effect the following day.
Implementation is indicatively scheduled for 10 December 2026.
body: The scheme meeting gave the infrastructure investor overwhelming support: more than 273 million votes for and fewer than 300,000 against, with 90.53% of shareholders present and voting in favour.
Once the court approves the scheme, oOh!media's shares will be suspended from trading on the ASX, with a record date of 3 December.
The deal follows a wave of private-capital interest in OOH, including Mubadala Capital's acquisition of Clear Channel Outdoor.
items.relevance: Private infrastructure investors now see OOH as long-term, cash-generating infrastructure. That valuation case is useful when discussing long concessions with airports and transport authorities.

pitch.line: 99.89% of votes cast backed I Squared Capital's A$1.68-a-share takeover of oOh!media (ASX announcement, November 2026).

items.dek: 254 JCDecaux screens in Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius are now available to programmatic buyers, offering more than 163 million impressions a month.
items.source: Billboard Insider
keyPoints: VIOOH and JCDecaux have opened 254 Baltic screens to programmatic buying, with more than 163 million monthly impressions.
Tallinn contributes 61 screens and 75m+ impressions, Riga 83 screens and Vilnius 110.
The Riga inventory includes the Origo 3D screen.
The launch brings Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania into VIOOH's international supply.
body: VIOOH, JCDecaux's programmatic platform, announced the partnership with JCDecaux Baltics in London on 3 November. Buyers can now reach capital-city screens in all three Baltic states through their usual demand-side platforms.
Tallinn's smaller network generates the most impressions, at more than 75 million a month, reflecting high-footfall sites.
The move extends programmatic DOOH into smaller European markets, where international advertisers have previously had to buy direct.
items.relevance: Programmatic access makes smaller markets easy to add to pan-European campaigns. Sellers can pitch the Baltics as a low-friction extension for brands already buying DOOH programmatically elsewhere.

items.headline: Pittsburgh's airport authority signs a 20-year billboard deal

keyPoints: The Allegheny County Airport Authority, which runs Pittsburgh International and Allegheny County Airport, has signed a 20-year billboard land lease with Steel City Billboards.
Six new structures, mixing digital and static faces, are being built along Lebanon Church Road and Route 885 in West Mifflin.

No financial terms were disclosed.

Steel City Billboards, a family-owned Pittsburgh company, says the project is one of its largest infrastructure investments. Formetco is supplying the digital displays.
The billboards target commuters, residents and airport traffic in Pittsburgh's South Hills.

brief: AI search is turning into an ad market, but not yet a good one: ChatGPT placements have passed 200,000, while WARC reports they deliver less than a sixth of Google Search's value for money.
Brand value is consolidating around technology (Interbrand puts the top 100 at $3.9trn), and Kantar warns that creator engagement rarely builds the brand itself.
In the US, a record $11.87bn midterm cycle and Lamar's 42% programmatic growth show where national money is flowing; in Australia, word of mouth beats paid media six to one for product trial.
Diary: Schiphol's €426m advertising tender closes on 20 November.

items.headline: ChatGPT ads pass 200,000 placements, but the returns lag far behind search
items.dek: Adthena has tracked a near-sixfold rise in advertisers on ChatGPT ahead of the first AI-driven holiday season. A separate study reported by WARC finds those ads deliver less than a sixth of the value of paid Google Search.
items.source: Adthena, via GlobeNewswire; WARC
keyPoints: Adthena logged 204,489 ChatGPT ad placements between June and September 2026, and the advertiser base grew almost sixfold in two months.
Apparel, consumer electronics and travel account for roughly 95% of placements.
Ads cluster around early-stage research: 83% of beauty ads and 69% of travel ads appeared against such queries.
Ads in Google's AI Overviews rose 536% year on year in Australia, 160% in the UK and EU and 89% in the US.
A study reported by WARC finds ChatGPT ads offer less than a sixth of the value for money of paid Google Search.
body: Advertising inside AI assistants has moved from experiment to land-grab in a matter of months. Adthena's tracking shows more than 200,000 ChatGPT placements over the summer, heavily concentrated in apparel, electronics and travel, and skewed towards the research phase of the purchase journey rather than the point of sale.

Google is moving just as fast. Paid placements in its AI Overviews have surged across markets, most dramatically in Australia, and Adthena counts more than 175,000 in the US alone, again led by apparel and consumer electronics.

The economics, however, remain unproven. A new study covered by WARC on 4 November concludes that ChatGPT ads trail paid search by a wide margin on performance, and that advertising alone is unlikely to fund free access to the service under current conditions.
items.relevance: Budgets are being lured into AI answers that are still unproven on returns. Position OOH as the verified, brand-safe reach medium that sits alongside AI discovery, especially for travel and electronics clients now testing ChatGPT ads.

pitch.line: ChatGPT ads deliver less than a sixth of the value for money of paid Google Search, according to a study reported by WARC in November 2026.

items.headline: Kantar: AI now answers for your brand, and creator content rarely builds it
items.dek: Kantar's five shifts for 2027 argue that brands must win inside AI assistants and stop mistaking engagement for brand building. Only 6% of creator content works for both the platform and the brand.
items.source: Kantar, Kantar Forward 2026

figures.label: Used an AI assistant (6 months, 12 markets)
Creator content working for brand and platform
Innovations that fail to build brand meaning
Growth odds for high Future Power brands

keyPoints: 82% of people across 12 markets have used an AI assistant in the past six months, so brands must be present, accurate and distinctive in AI-generated answers.
Only 6% of creator content performs for both the platform and the brand; Kantar warns that engagement is not brand building.
Two in three innovations fail to build meaning for the brand behind them.
Brands with strong Future Power are four times as likely to grow value share the following year.
Kantar is pushing earlier testing, including 'consumer twins' built from past research respondents.
body: Kantar's annual outlook, drawn from its Blueprint for Brand Growth and presented at its first Kantar Forward broadcast, frames 2027 around a new gatekeeper. With more than four in five consumers now using AI assistants, a brand increasingly reaches people through a single synthesised answer, and must be visible and correctly described within it.

The firm is equally pointed about social. Its research suggests creator content often wins attention without strengthening the brand, and only a small fraction serves both. Kraft Heinz is piloting Kantar's LINK AI to tie social performance to long-term brand effects.
The remaining shifts concern speed: shaping launches before money is spent, bringing consumers into decisions earlier, and testing ideas on digital replicas of real respondents.
items.relevance: The 'engagement is not brand building' line is a gift for OOH sellers. Use it with clients over-indexed on creators to argue for broadcast-scale, brand-building presence in streets, transport and airports.

pitch.line: Only 6% of creator content works for both the platform and the brand, according to Kantar's 2026 research.

items.pdfNote: Kantar has published the summary online; the underlying Blueprint for Brand Growth data is not available as a public PDF.

items.headline: Interbrand: technology takes half of the world's brand value as carmakers slide
items.dek: The top 100 brands are worth $3.9trn, up 8.1%, with technology accounting for 48%. NVIDIA enters the top ten while Tesla and the German car marques fall sharply.
items.source: Interbrand, Best Global Brands 2026, via MediaNews4U
keyPoints: Apple remains first at $514.6bn, followed by Microsoft ($443.7bn), Google ($389.3bn) and Amazon ($351.8bn).
NVIDIA rises 71.5% to $74bn and enters the top ten for the first time; Spotify (+37.8%) and Uber (+34.7%) are also strong risers.
Entertainment overtakes automotive as the second most valuable sector.
Tesla falls 37.8% and drops from 28th to 50th; Volkswagen, Honda, Toyota, Mercedes-Benz and BMW all lose between 18% and 23%.
New entrants include Zurich, Hitachi, GE HealthCare and Hewlett Packard Enterprise.
body: Interbrand's annual league table confirms how far artificial intelligence has reshaped corporate value. Technology now accounts for almost half of the top 100's worth, with Google and YouTube each growing by more than a fifth and NVIDIA leaping into the top ten.

The losers are concentrated in automotive. Every major carmaker on the list lost value, led by Tesla, as electric-vehicle competition and tariffs bit. Entertainment, by contrast, climbed to second place among sectors.
Interbrand argues that as technology becomes widely accessible, brands must turn their strength into commercial advantage rather than relying on reach alone.
items.relevance: Use the risers list to prioritise prospecting: AI, streaming and platform brands are flush and building awareness. Carmakers under pressure may need persuading that brand-building media is the answer, not a cut.

pitch.line: The world's 100 most valuable brands are worth $3.9trn in 2026, up 8.1%, and technology accounts for 48% of that value (Interbrand).

items.headline: Euromonitor: 2027 will be the year shoppers buy confidence
items.dek: Euromonitor's annual trends report finds consumers trusting brands, AI and the future less, and rewarding whatever feels dependable and within their control.
items.source: Euromonitor International, Top Global Consumer Trends 2027
keyPoints: Five trends: Shelf Assured, Reluctant Reliance, Peer Powered, Mode-Switching and Future Tense.
Shelf Assured: more than half of consumers buy only from brands they fully trust, and 72% worry about rising prices. Reliability is the new value proposition.
Reluctant Reliance: 81% use generative AI for daily tasks, but only 19% see it as a highly trustworthy source of shopping information.
Peer Powered: nearly three-quarters trust recommendations from friends and family when buying.
Future Tense: 38% think the world will be more dangerous within five years, so people favour immediate, tangible value over long-term promises.
body: Euromonitor's head of innovation, Ali Angus, sums up the report: consumers are no longer simply buying products, they are looking for confidence. The thread running through all five trends is control, whether over a shopping basket, an AI assistant or an uncertain future.

The report draws on Euromonitor's Passport data and its Voice of the Consumer surveys. Its message for marketers is that trust is no longer an abstract brand value but something consumers check shelf by shelf, interaction by interaction.
items.relevance: Consistency, visibility and real-world presence are what reassure a wary shopper. OOH's always-on, unskippable public presence is a natural fit for the 'Shelf Assured' brief, and its brand-safe context answers the scepticism about AI and algorithms.

pitch.line: Only 19% of consumers see AI as a highly trustworthy source of shopping advice, even though 81% use it every day (Euromonitor, 2027 trends).

items.headline: Hard to influence is the new cool, says TBWA's Backslash
items.dek: A study of consumers in the US and UK finds most now assume viral hits are manufactured, and rate a distinct point of view far above mass popularity.
items.source: TBWA Backslash, Becoming Uninfluenced

figures.label: Say hard to influence is aspirational

keyPoints: 62% say being hard to influence is more aspirational than being an influencer.
When something goes viral, 42% first assume a brand engineered it and 33% suspect bots. Only 25% assume people genuinely love it.
Asked what makes a brand culturally relevant, respondents ranked a distinct point of view first and mass popularity last.
The report names the anxiety 'taste paranoia': the fear that one's preferences are really the product of algorithms.
body: TBWA's cultural intelligence unit draws three lessons for brands: trust grows the further you get from the feed, things that feel genuinely discovered are now the most desirable, and brands should build places for culture to happen rather than try to manufacture it.
The research combines expert interviews and cultural analysis with a survey of more than 700 people in the US and UK.
items.relevance: A strong argument for the physical world: discovery in the street, the station or the airport feels unengineered in a way the feed no longer does. Use it with brands that are rethinking heavy influencer budgets.

pitch.line: Only a quarter of consumers believe a viral hit is genuinely popular; 42% assume a brand engineered it (TBWA Backslash, 2026).

items.headline: IAB Europe: retail media buyers want proof, and sellers can't yet supply it
items.dek: Seven in ten European buyers now have retailer partnerships of more than a year, but only 12% consider their strategies sophisticated. Measurement is the main brake on investment.
items.source: IAB Europe, Attitudes to Retail Media Report 2026, via ExchangeWire
keyPoints: 71% of European buyers have partnered with retailers for more than a year, up from 51% in 2024.
61% cite a lack of measurement and reporting as a leading barrier; concern about data availability jumped from 31% to 58% in a year.
Buyers want unified online and offline reporting (66%), new-to-brand measurement (63%) and incrementality (57%).
Only 49% now choose ROAS as a desired metric, down from 89% in 2025.
58% of buyers want multi-touch attribution, but only 31% of sellers offer it.
body: Retail media in Europe has matured in adoption but not in accountability. IAB Europe's third annual survey of 150 buyers and sellers, which for the first time includes a meaningful sample from the Middle East and North Africa, shows long-term retailer partnerships becoming the norm while confidence in the numbers falls.

The shift in metrics is striking. Return on ad spend, once the default, has lost its grip, and buyers are now asking for incrementality, new-to-brand measures and, above all, a single view across online and in-store activity.
Sellers say they are responding: 63% plan to improve measurement within a year, and two-thirds are building AI-powered campaign tools.
items.relevance: The demand for unified online and offline reporting is an opening for in-store and near-store DOOH. Position retail and airport screens as the physical extension of retail media networks, with measurement built in.

pitch.line: 66% of European retail media buyers now prioritise unified online and offline reporting, according to IAB Europe's 2026 study.

items.headline: US midterms set an $11.87bn political advertising record
items.dek: AdImpact's tally makes 2025–26 the most expensive cycle ever, ahead of the 2024 presidential race. Connected TV more than doubled on the last midterms.
items.source: AdImpact, via The Current
keyPoints: AdImpact puts the 2025–26 cycle at $11.87bn, above the $11.2bn spent in the 2024 presidential cycle.
Broadcast TV took about $5.8bn, nearly half of the total; CTV took $2.6bn, or 22%.
CTV spending more than doubled on the 2022 midterms.
Spending far outstripped AdImpact's own September 2025 projection of $10bn.
OOH benefited too: Lamar expects more than $40m of political revenue this year, more than double 2022.
body: Tuesday's elections closed the most expensive campaign in American history. AdImpact's final count is well ahead of the previous midterm cycle in 2022 and narrowly above the 2024 presidential race, powered by heavily contested Senate and governor contests.

Broadcast television still captured the largest share, but the growth came from connected TV, which more than doubled on four years ago. Sport was a magnet, accounting for the majority of traditional TV political spend, according to iSpot data.
With the money now spent, local TV and CTV inventory will be released in November and December, which could soften pricing for commercial advertisers in the holiday quarter.
items.relevance: Expect US media owners to report a political comedown in 2027 comps. For global clients planning the US, the release of TV inventory may tempt budgets back to screens; keep OOH's reach-per-dollar case to hand.

pitch.line: US political advertising reached a record $11.87bn in the 2025–26 cycle, and CTV spending more than doubled on 2022 (AdImpact).
